001-250760:
The applicant, Bakur Kiguradze, a Georgian national born in 1955 and living in Tbilisi, is an entrepreneur, a member of the Georgian Academy of Energy and a published author. In 2011, after in camera proceedings, he was convicted of espionage and sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment. On 5 December 2012 Parliament declared him a “political prisoner,” along with others. He was released under an Amnesty Act adopted on 12 January 2013. After he requested reopening, a full retrial was conducted; on 16 July 2018 the 2011 conviction was quashed and he was acquitted of all charges.

In 2020, media outlets reported that several companies and entrepreneurs had donated over GEL 2 million to the ruling Georgian Dream party in the first quarter of that year. The applicant was reported to have donated GEL 50,000 (approximately EUR 14,500). Media outlets and opposition politicians questioned his motives and those of other contributors. In that context, MP I.A., interviewed apparently inside the Parliament building, said that corrupt practices were deterring investment and, regarding Georgian Dream’s attitude towards spies for Russia, stated that not only Kiguradze but other individuals convicted of espionage had been released by Georgian Dream as political prisoners, and that no spies had been revealed since; “these people are the political partners of Georgian Dream.”

On 15 July 2020 the applicant instituted civil proceedings against I.A., Mtavari Arkhi Ltd, TV Pirveli Ltd and RFE/RL’s Georgian service. He sought a declaration that he had been discriminated against, retraction of the allegedly defamatory statement, and non-pecuniary damages. He argued that the defendants had disseminated defamatory content referring to his earlier arrest and conviction for espionage for Russia and his release as a political prisoner, but had failed to mention that he had been fully acquitted in the reopened proceedings.

I.A. asked for discontinuation based on parliamentary immunity under the Constitution and the Freedom of Speech and Expression Act. He submitted that his statement referred to Parliament’s decree declaring certain individuals, including the applicant, political prisoners; because that was a political decision, his statement was a political argument made in the exercise of parliamentary duties, not defamation. The applicant replied that the criminal case had been re-examined in 2018 and all espionage charges dismissed, a fact known to I.A. While accepting that an MP could assess Parliament’s decisions, he maintained that the statement portrayed him as a convicted Russian spy released as a political prisoner and was slanderous.

On 5 October 2021 the Tbilisi City Court discontinued the proceedings against I.A. It found that the statement had been made in the context of political expression and in the exercise of his duties as an MP. It referred to the Constitution, Article 10 of the Convention, the Freedom of Speech and Expression Act, the domestic definition of defamation, Supreme Court practice on distinguishing facts from value judgments, and Parliament’s declaration that the applicant was a political prisoner. It noted that I.A. had been an MP since 2016, that the statement was aired on 19 May 2020, and that section 5 of the Act exempted statements made as part of political debate or in relation to MP duties. It also referred to Parliament decree no. 76 of 5 December 2012, which listed the applicant among political prisoners. Applying Supreme Court guidance, it concluded that the statement contained both statements of fact and value judgments, fell within section 5, and allowed discontinuation.

The applicant lodged an interlocutory appeal, reiterating his arguments. On 24 January 2023 a three-judge panel of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, sitting as final instance, upheld the lower decision in a 13-page ruling, taking note of his arguments but repeating the lower court’s reasoning. The decision was served on 23 February 2023. The proceedings ended on 15 May 2023 in respect of RFE/RL’s Georgian service; they appear to be ongoing as regards the remaining parties.

Domestic law provided that Article 39 § 3 of the Constitution exempts MPs from liability for views expressed inside or outside Parliament while performing their duties. Section 5 of the Freedom of Speech and Expression Act provides that statements made as part of political debate or in relation to MP duties do not incur defamation liability; the court determines this at a preliminary hearing and may terminate proceedings under Articles 209 and 273 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Termination bars a new claim concerning the same parties, subject and grounds, and is appealable under Article 274. In a decision of 17 May 2023 (no. ას-57-2023), the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court upheld rejection of an MP’s discontinuation request, finding that the statements went beyond mere political debate and amounted to an accusation of a criminal offence lacking sufficient factual basis. The applicant lodged application no. 25784/23 against Georgia on 23 June 2023, relying on Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention.
001-250883:
The applicant, Ms Elisabeth Gertrude Eikenaar, a Dutch national born in 1960 and living in Hellevoetsluis, lodged an application against the Netherlands concerning the alleged disproportionate use of force by a police officer against her late partner, E.C.U. She relied on Article 3 of the Convention.

On 23 November 2016, at about 4.20 p.m., the Rotterdam police control centre received reports from neighbours that E.C.U. was behaving in a confused manner in the street, acting aggressively and swearing at passers-by. Five police officers, including a dog handler, were assigned. They were informed that E.C.U. had a prior record of violence, threats and drug offences. When the police arrived, E.C.U. had returned home. Officers heard him shouting wildly and aggressively, with unintelligible speech, and thought he might be destroying furniture and posing a danger to himself and others. They asked him several times to open the door; he did not respond and reacted hysterically. The officers decided to enter, discussed their approach, and forced the door with a battering ram. They identified themselves and used the “shield procedure”. E.C.U. showed himself with his hands stretched out and complied with instructions to approach and lie on the floor.

While on the floor, as two officers tried to handcuff him, E.C.U. resisted and yelled loudly. A third officer sat on his back and buttocks, but he kicked and swung his arms. Several officers tried to restrain him. Officer X placed his knee on E.C.U.’s neck but could not pull his right arm from under his body. Officer X then punched E.C.U. twice on the ribs below the right shoulder. When E.C.U. did not react, Officer X removed his knee and punched him with a closed fist on the back of the head. E.C.U. then moved his arm and aimed a hit at Officer X, enabling an armlock. After a warning, a police dog bit E.C.U. twice on the calf. Later, an officer sitting on E.C.U.’s back punched him twice on the left side; both arms were then handcuffed behind his back. He gradually calmed down. After arrest, he was taken to a police station, where he soon appeared to lose consciousness. Medical assistance was called, but resuscitation was unsuccessful. He died at 6.05 p.m., aged 58.

The pathologist’s final report of 20 April 2017 concluded that death could well be explained by a high cocaine concentration, a cocaine-related death, and no causal link between police force and death was established. The autopsy noted superficial skin lesions, hematomas and a bruise on the head and face, including on the back of the head, lesions and bruises on the arms, elbows and left wrist, dog-bite wounds, and four broken ribs attributed to resuscitation. A National Criminal Investigations Department report of 19 May 2017 stated that all involved officers were trained and certified to use force. On 5 July 2017, the Chief Public Prosecutor closed the investigation, finding the force necessary and proportionate given E.C.U.’s fierce resistance and no indication that violence caused or contributed to death. No prosecution was instituted.

On 2 October 2017, the applicant lodged a complaint under Article 12 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the decision not to prosecute Officer X for (aggravated) assault, arguing that the force, including the punch to the head, was unnecessary and disproportionate and unlawful given E.C.U.’s confused state. The complaint did not address the death or other officers. The Chief Public Prosecutor recommended dismissal on 6 November 2017, and the Advocate-General recommended dismissal on 5 February 2018. On 18 April 2018, the Court of Appeal held a hearing; the applicant repeated her arguments, questioned whether the police had entered to render assistance under the Police Act, and raised a systemic problem regarding confused individuals. On 9 May 2018, the Court of Appeal dismissed the complaint. It found that E.C.U. had resisted violently, that warnings were given, and that the file showed no relationship between death and force. It noted uncertainty over the legal basis for the arrest but found no one-sided or excessive force. It considered that Officer X should have refrained from the punch to the head, but held that, in the circumstances, there was no criminal offence requiring prosecution. No appeal lay.
001-250890:
A.P., a Polish national born in 1978, lives in Northampton, United Kingdom, in a same-sex relationship with E.K., also Polish. A.P. gave birth to R.P. on 27 November 2014 in London. R.P., born in 2014 and living in Northampton, is also a Polish national. The applicants stated that R.P.’s biological father was a man whom A.P. and E.K. met through an internet sperm-donor matching portal and that he did not wish to take part in the child’s upbringing. R.P.’s original birth certificate named A.P. as mother and E.K. as parent. The applicants’ complaints under Article 8 alone and with Article 14 concerned the refusal of Polish authorities to register the foreign birth certificate.

On 23 January 2015 A.P. applied to the Polish Consulate in London for a Polish passport for R.P. She submitted that the application was not accepted and that she received no written reply. On 1 April 2015 she applied again; the consulate requested a Polish birth certificate. On 7 May 2015 the Polish Consul in London said the passport application had been left unprocessed because no Polish birth certificate had been produced. On 29 July 2015 the Minister of the Interior rejected her complaint as unfounded. On 16 May 2016 the Warsaw Regional Administrative Court rejected the applicants’ complaint as inadmissible in law.

On 28 July 2015 the applicants applied to the Myszków Civil Status Registry to register/transcribe the child’s foreign birth certificate in Poland. On 18 August 2015 the Director refused. The Director stated that the authority did not examine the contents of a foreign certificate, but Polish law did not recognise same-sex parents; registration would be contrary to public policy; under Polish law the mother was the woman who gave birth and the father was a man; and it was impossible to register a certificate showing two women as parents. The decision relied on section 7 of the Private International Law Act 2011. The applicants appealed, relying on Article 8, the child’s best interests and the child’s uncertain legal situation.

On 9 October 2015 the Śląski Governor upheld the refusal. The Governor found that transcription could be refused if it contravened fundamental rules of Polish legal order; the foreign certificate was contrary to the Family and Custody Code; Polish law did not allow same-sex unions or adoption by same-sex couples; and the foreign certificate could still be used in Polish courts under Article 1138 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The first applicant appealed, alleging breach of the Constitution and discrimination against the child as a child in a same-sex family. On 6 April 2016 the Gliwice Regional Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It reasoned that registration would require a woman’s data to be entered in the “father” field, which was not possible; there was no registration of same-sex relationships or second-parent adoption for same-sex parents; and the public policy exception applied. It also stated that transcription was unnecessary because the child could rely on the foreign birth certificate before Polish authorities.

The first applicant lodged a cassation appeal, arguing that a Polish birth certificate was necessary to obtain a Polish passport, relying on the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the child’s best interests, and alleging discrimination based on the parents’ sexual orientation. On 18 June 2018 the Polish Human Rights Commissioner intervened, observing that under section 104(5) of the 2014 Law on Civil Status Records registration was required for a Polish identity document or PESEL number; that the child’s best interests had not been considered; and that the public policy clause had been applied automatically. On 20 June 2018 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the cassation appeal, holding that transcription would contravene the domestic legal order and that the child’s best interests were protected by the evidential value of the foreign document under Article 1138 CCP and the Supreme Court’s resolution of 20 November 2012 (III CZP 58/12).
001-250892:
The applicants are H’s mother (the first applicant), father (the second applicant), and maternal grandparents (the third and fourth applicants). The first applicant, a medical graduate and acupuncturist, had a history of psychiatric disorders; in 2010 she was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and compulsorily hospitalised, later receiving treatment and support from a mental-health centre until 2016. She met the second applicant online in 2014, visited him in Türkiye in August 2016, married him on 11 October 2016, and moved to Italy in November 2016 while pregnant.

On 3 July 2017, at 39 weeks pregnant, she threatened suicide and was taken to hospital. The baby was in breech position and a caesarean section was advised, but she refused. A psychiatric examination on 4 July found her lucid and of sound mind, and her decision was respected. The applicant, Abdulsattar Abdulbaset Allabed, a Syrian national born in 1973, lives in Aarhus. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment and ordered expelled with a permanent re-entry ban. On appeal, the High Court, by judgment of 9 February 2024, upheld the conviction, reduced the sentence to two years and six months, and ordered expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. It assessed Article 8 and found that he had laundered or attempted to launder DKK 10 million from organised drug-related offences. He entered Denmark at 39 and had been lawfully resident for about eight and a half years; his Danish skills were limited and his ties with Denmark very limited, with only two supermarket work placements, no regular employment, and social welfare benefits. It found a significant risk of similar future offences. It considered him strongly tied culturally to Syria, where he spoke Arabic, was a trained engineer, had worked in construction, and had a business partner. His spouse and seven children lived in Denmark; two minor children lived at home, and all except one child derived residence rights from him. The High Court found that a permanent re-entry ban would certainly be contrary to Article 8, but that expulsion with a six-year ban would not.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that as a Syrian national in visa main group 5, his chances of being granted a visa to re-enter Denmark were purely theoretical, so the six-year ban was de facto permanent. He referred to Sharafane v. Denmark. By judgment of 29 January 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the High Court. It noted the sentence concerned laundering DKK 9,135,500 and attempted laundering of DKK 900,000, handling stolen goods of about DKK 650,000, and other offences over a long period. Although he had no prior convictions, the offences were serious and there was a significant recidivism risk. At 51, he had been lawfully resident for about eight and a half years; apart from family ties, his ties to Denmark were very limited, with limited Danish and little labour-market participation. His spouse was also Syrian. Two minor children lived at home and five adult children, two of whom lived at home; all had considerable ties to Denmark. The Supreme Court considered the spouse well equipped to live in Syria and the children aged 12 and 14 not ill-equipped, given their Syrian family background. If they stayed in Denmark, contact could be maintained through visits, if circumstances permitted, or by telephone or internet. It found the applicant a serious threat to public order and that the arguments for expulsion outweighed those against, so the six-year ban was not contrary to Denmark’s international obligations.

On 17 September 2025, the applicant was detained on remand and charged with further particularly serious money-laundering offences; that case is ongoing.

The Executive Order on Visas was amended on 12 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025, inserting section 16(7). It permits a visa for a person born and raised in Denmark, or who came as a young child, in main group 5, after a time-limited re-entry ban expires, if refusing a visa would violate the right to respect for private life under Denmark’s international obligations. Main group 5 includes Syria. The Danish Immigration Service stated that no applicants had yet relied on section 16(7). In another domestic case, the Supreme Court on 18 March 2025 examined a Somali national born in Denmark and found his prospects of a visa after a six-year ban were not purely theoretical in light of the amendment.

The seizure covered the entirety of the properties (1/1 shares), and a mortgage annotation was entered in the Land Register. The assets remained in the spouses’ possession. It found the order reasoned, the damage based on an expert report, and the enforcement report signed without objection. It considered joint spousal property to belong to both spouses without fixed shares, the measure provisional, and the applicant still able to exercise ownership attributes except sale. The applications were lodged by five individuals against Russia and/or Ukraine: Volodymyr Bazhenov, Svitlana Sklyarenko, Oleksandr Bornyakov and Anatoliy Agafonov, Ukrainian nationals, and Yelena Melnik, a Russian national. They complained about the cancellation by Russian authorities of their titles to plots of land in Sevastopol, Crimea, originally transferred into private ownership by Ukrainian authorities and reclaimed as public forest land. They relied on Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; the fourth applicant relied only on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They also complained in substance under Article 13.

In 2009 and 2010 the Sevastopol City Administration (SCA) and Sevastopol City Council (SCC) decided to transfer various public land plots into private ownership for building individual dachas. The grants concerned dacha cooperatives “Selena”, “Blagopoluchnyy” and “Terra-Yug” for the first to fourth applicants, or one individual in the fifth applicant’s case. Between 2010 and 2014 Ukrainian authorities conducted inquiries into the allocations; Ukrainian administrative courts confirmed the SCA’s decisions as lawful, and criminal investigation authorities discontinued inquiries for lack of offence. The first and third applicants were original allottees; the other applicants purchased plots from private parties. The applicants registered their titles at various times. The first and second applicants registered after Russia asserted jurisdiction over Crimea and did so under Russian law. The third, fourth and fifth applicants initially registered under Ukrainian law and later also under Russian law.

Between 2015 and 2017 various Russian Sevastopol authorities—including the “Government of Sevastopol”, the Sevastopol department of property and land relations, and local prosecutors—brought actions against the first, second, fourth and fifth applicants in the Balaklava District Court of Sevastopol to cancel their titles and return the land to public property. The third applicant was involved as a third party in the proceedings against the second applicant. The authorities argued that the 2009–2010 transfers violated the then-applicable Ukrainian law because the plots were forest lands that could not be privatised under Article 84 of the Land Code of Ukraine, and that the SCA and SCC had acted ultra vires. They said the initial allocation was unlawful and succeeding titles were void, seeking return of the land to the Russian Federation under Articles 301 and 302 of the Russian Civil Code. The applicants argued the allocations and subsequent transfers were lawful. The first and fifth applicants also asserted the claims were time-barred. The third applicant submitted that the second applicant had acquired her land in good faith.

The Balaklava Court allowed the claims, cancelled the first, second, fourth and fifth applicants’ titles, and ordered return of the land to the State as public property without compensation. On limitation, it reasoned that the claimants were not successors of the Ukrainian authorities and only became aware of the title issues after Crimea’s annexation. Appeals, including by the third applicant as a third party, were unsuccessful; final domestic decision dates appear in the appended table.

After her title was cancelled, the second applicant sued the third applicant for the sum paid for the land. On 4 December 2017 the Nakhimovskiy District Court of Sevastopol, relying on Article 461 of the Russian Civil Code, allowed the claim in full and ordered the third applicant to pay RUB 2,250,945.94, including interest and expenses (about EUR 32,200), plus a court fee of RUB 302.22. The third applicant appealed, arguing she had not known of third-party rights at the time of sale and was not responsible for the subsequent cancellation. On 19 March 2018 the Sevastopol City Court dismissed the appeals and upheld the judgment; no further appeal was made.

The record also refers to Ukrainian land law, the Temporarily Occupied Territories Act, Russian Civil Code provisions, Russian constitutional law and Sevastopol measures recognising pre-existing title documents, as well as international materials concerning occupation law, State responsibility, and reported expropriations in Crimea and Sevastopol.

The applicant, Mr Serghei Paniușchin, a Moldovan national born in 1982 and living in Chișinău, lodged an application against the Republic of Moldova. He was represented by A. Balan, a lawyer practising in Chișinău. The case arose from domestic court proceedings concerning his claim against a private individual, S.L., for repayment of a loan of EUR 19,062 and further interest of EUR 22,644.

On 3 May 2017 the applicant instituted court proceedings against S.L. in the Moldovan courts. He paid one fifth of the court fees due—MDL 5,000, equivalent at the material time to EUR 235—and requested the court to exempt him from paying the remainder. He argued that his family had financial difficulties. He stated that the sole revenue of his family of four was his monthly salary of MDL 4,613 (EUR 217), because his wife was unemployed and had had no income in 2016. He submitted the birth certificates of his minor children and payslips for 2016 and the beginning of 2017.

On 10 May 2017 the Chișinău District Court gave the applicant 15 days to pay the remainder of the court fees, which totalled MDL 20,000 (EUR 942), after which it would examine his case. The applicant reiterated his request to be exempted from paying the remainder. He also submitted a certificate issued by the Tax Inspectorate attesting that his wife had had no income in 2016 and that his youngest child was only one year old. He further argued that, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, for the first semester of 2016 the minimum subsistence level for a family of four was MDL 7,888 (EUR 386), which exceeded his income. He asserted that he was unable to pay the court fees in full.

On 5 June 2017 the Chișinău District Court rejected the applicant’s request for exemption and refused to examine his case on account of his failure to pay the court fees in full. The court noted that the applicant had not presented proof of his inability to pay the court fees, such as copies of the balance of his bank accounts or any information regarding his assets. The court also noted that the applicant was represented by a lawyer of his own choosing, which, in the court’s view, implied that he was financially capable of covering the court fees.

The applicant appealed against that decision. In his appeal he reiterated his inability to pay the court fees in full and relied on the evidence submitted to the first-instance court. He noted that the amount of fees already paid had been substantial, given his financial situation.

On 26 October 2017 the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s decision and held that the applicant had failed to prove his precarious financial situation. That decision was final.

The applicant complained that the domestic courts’ refusal to examine his claim, owing to his failure to pay court fees, limited his right of access to a court. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 25 April 2018.
001-251196:
Ms Renata Karičková, a Czech national born in 1972 living in Sokolov, alleged that she was attacked by private individuals for allegedly racist reasons and that the ensuing investigation was ineffective, influenced by racist stereotypes, and failed to uncover the racist motive. The Czech Government was the respondent.

On 23 July 2021, in Sokolov, an altercation arose between local Roma residents and a visiting group of 15 people on a boating holiday, some identified as football ultras. Several members of the visiting group had previous convictions, including for disorderly conduct, performing a Nazi salute, and expressing sympathies for a movement suppressing human rights. J.P., a Roma resident, asked the group for cigarettes; a verbal argument escalated. O.Š. chased J.P., then hit 13-year-old M.B. in the face, reportedly saying “you Gypsy motherfucker”. A wider physical altercation followed, with objects thrown, fist fights, and injuries. A deaf and mute Roma resident, E.G., suffered a broken arm; the applicant’s husband E.K. suffered a knife wound; her son T.K. and others were hit. The applicant was struck with a brick, causing bruises and swelling and inability to work for 15 days. Shortly afterwards she recorded herself telling police she wanted to file a criminal complaint against “the tall man standing over there”; police did not respond. On 25 July 2021 local Roma organised a demonstration alleging police protected the attackers.

On 23 July 2021 the Sokolov District Police opened an investigation into disorderly conduct and bodily harm. The applicant was interviewed on 24 July 2021 without legal representation and was not asked to describe her attacker. On 4 August 2021 her lawyer requested notification of investigative steps. Roma witnesses reported racist slurs such as “black bastards” and “black scum”; interviews of visiting group members did not ask about those slurs and referred to Roma as “Gypsies”. O.Š. admitted hitting M.B. On 26 August 2021 he was charged with disorderly conduct. On 12 October 2021 police closed proceedings concerning the applicant and E.G., finding no perpetrator identified.

On 15 October 2021 the applicant sought review, stating she had never said she could not identify her attacker and providing video evidence. On 23 December 2021 the district prosecutor ordered further investigation and an identity parade if she and E.G. confirmed they could identify. On 5 January 2022 the Sokolov District Court found O.Š. guilty of disorderly conduct for attacking M.B. and others, imposing a fine; the applicant was not identified as an aggrieved party. On 6 January 2022 she complained against Officer S.K., alleging biased misinterpretation, failure to conduct an identity parade or consider video evidence, and failure to notify her.

On 14 January 2022 the applicant’s and E.G.’s case was severed from the main case. On 11 February 2022 the applicant described her attacker as about 190 cm, the tallest of the group, with dark hair, short beard, striped T-shirt and jean shorts, and said she could identify him. On 2 May 2022 police again closed her case, finding she had confused individuals and her injury was below the criminal threshold. The district prosecutor dismissed her review on 17 June 2022. On 27 September 2022 the regional prosecutor approved, doubting Roma statements, stating her description corresponded to O.Š., whose further prosecution was barred, and finding no need to investigate a racist motive. On 5 December 2022 the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal complaining of an ineffective, biased investigation, lack of participation, retaliatory separation of her case, and failure to investigate hate-crime indicators. On 1 November 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed it as manifestly ill-founded.
001-251247:
The applicants are Ms Audrey Carmen Manuela Ubeda, a French national born in 1983, and her minor children A.P. and M.P., French nationals born in 2011 and 2014, living in Italy. The first applicant also acted for her children. They complained of the Italian authorities’ alleged failure to effectively investigate her complaints of domestic and sexual violence, delays in criminal proceedings and effects on them, and alleged inaction by the Juvenile Court in custody proceedings; the record states issues under Articles 3 and 8.

On 16 April 2021 the first applicant complained to the police against G.P., the father of her children and former cohabitant. She alleged physical and psychological violence against her and the children between 2018 and 2020, aggravated sexual violence, threats, a climate of terror and economic violence. She described belt beatings and slaps from 2018 to 2020 and death threats. On 19 October 2019, during the third child’s birthday, G.P. allegedly held a knife to her throat in front of her mother and cousin, saying he would appear on television, alluding to femicide. She alleged psychological insults and no contribution to household expenses. She alleged multiple rapes from March to September 2020 in the marital bed where the third child slept; an April 2016 forced anal intercourse; and masturbation while watching her clean until she agreed to sex.

On 22 April 2021 Naples police referred the case to the Benevento prosecutor. On 23 April 2021 the prosecutor opened proceedings and sought interviews, documentation and witnesses. Police interviewed the first applicant with a psychologist, collected messages, and interviewed the children and two witnesses. On 24 May 2021 the applicants were placed in a protected shelter. On 5 November 2021 the prosecutor requested discontinuance, calling the knife episode a “bad joke”, the blows to the children disciplinary measures within parental authority, and the sexual violence unestablished. He stated it was difficult to show the husband knew of lack of consent and that it was normal for men to overcome minimum resistance. The first applicant objected; on 18 January 2022 the objection was upheld. A hearing on 1 April 2022 was adjourned for six months, the investigation was extended, and a new prosecutor assigned. On 13 July 2022 the applicants were examined via incidente probatorio. On 18 November 2022 investigative conclusions were issued. On 6 March 2023 committal was requested. On 30 October 2023 the case was adjourned to 12 February 2024. On 12 February 2024 G.P. was committed for trial, with the first hearing set for 17 September 2024, on charges of sexual assault against the first applicant and ill-treatment of all three applicants. On 17 September 2024 the case was adjourned to 14 January 2025; no hearing had been held at the time of observations.

In civil proceedings, on 6 May 2021 the first applicant asked the Naples Juvenile Court for sole custody, removal of G.P.’s parental responsibility, permission to leave Italy for France, and maintenance, citing the assaults. A guardian was appointed on 16 July 2021 and a social services report requested. At hearings on 14 March and 8 April 2022 the applicants reported abuse. Supervised visits took place between April and June 2022; the children expressed fear and refused their father, and on the last visit G.P. behaved aggressively while the children hid in a car boot. Reports described distress and need for a neuropsychiatrist. On 17 June 2022 the Juvenile Court interim suspended G.P.’s parental responsibility and supervised meetings, required psychological support, confirmed shelter placement, and adjourned to 16 December 2022. G.P. appealed; the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 14 April 2023. Later reports in 2022-2023 described severe distress, shelter restrictions, the children’s wish to leave, and the third child’s faecal incontinence. A hearing on 6 July 2023 was adjourned to 9 May 2024. Urgent requests in July and August 2023 sought travel to France; August travel was granted. On 9 May 2024 the Juvenile Court deprived G.P. of parental responsibility but made no express ruling on removal from the shelter, France, sole custody or maintenance; social services monitoring continued. The applicants left the shelter on 8 July 2024.
001-251251:
The applicants are two Ukrainian nationals, Mr Pavlo Yevgenovych Kolesnyk (born 1971) and Mr Sergiy Mytrofanovych Smelnytskyy (born 1975). At the time of the most recent communication with the Court they were in detention in Kharkiv. They were represented by Mr Y. Vyshnevetskyy, and the Government by its Agent, Ms M. Sokorenko. Their applications were lodged on 28 and 29 May 2023.

The context was Russia’s full-scale military attack on Ukraine from 24 February 2022, the introduction of martial law, and heavy urban warfare in Kharkiv. On 29 July 2022 the Security Service of Ukraine arrested the applicants and notified them of suspicion that on 27 July 2022 they had filmed Ukrainian military fortifications and equipment in Kharkiv and shared the material on Telegram channels used by Russian intelligence. The offence was initially classified under Article 114-2 § 3 of the Criminal Code, covering unauthorised dissemination of information about Ukrainian military positions during wartime. According to the charges, the first applicant drove while the second filmed with a camera mounted on the car; the footage made it possible to locate the positions, and the first applicant transmitted it to the Telegram channels.

On 1 August 2022 the Kyivskyi District Court of Kharkiv ordered both applicants’ pre-trial detention. It found reasonable suspicion based on digital material and witness statements identifying them as driving a particular car in the relevant Kharkiv area. It also found risks of absconding, aggravated by the severity of punishment faced, influencing witnesses or otherwise interfering with the investigation, and reoffending. The court considered their personal circumstances but concluded that no other preventive measure would suffice. It set alternative bail of 372,150 Ukrainian hryvnias (about 9,800 euros) for each applicant, which was paid on 2 August 2022.

On 3 August 2022 the SBU investigator reclassified the offence as treason under Article 111 of the Criminal Code and asked for detention without bail. The investigator said the investigation showed the applicants had disseminated information to help Russia conduct subversive activities, so the acts could not remain classified under Article 114-2 § 3. He also noted they were former police officers who knew investigative methods, could influence witnesses or hinder the investigation, were aware of the offence’s gravity and the wartime complexity of the case, and could flee to Russia or occupied Ukrainian territory or commit further national-security offences.

On the same day, the District Court ordered detention without bail in two similar decisions. It found reasonable suspicion based on the earlier evidence and additional reports, and the same risks. It referred to the Wartime Detention Clause (Article 176 § 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) and the Exceptions to Mandatory Bail Clause (Article 183 § 4). At that time, the unauthorised-publication offence was not listed among the offences covered by those clauses, but treason was; the unauthorised-publication offence was added by Law no. 2531-IX of 16 August 2022.

The applicants appealed, arguing there was no evidence for reasonable suspicion or the risks and relying on their family circumstances and prior police service. The Kharkiv Court of Appeal rejected the first applicant’s appeal on 15 September 2022 and the second applicant’s on 29 September 2022, largely endorsing the lower court’s reasons.

The investigator later sought extensions, citing further investigative steps such as forensic analysis. In a 17 December 2022 extension application, the investigator alleged a risk of evidence destruction because the video had been deleted from the phone’s main storage, as had the chat room and participants, and because the second applicant or third parties had deleted his Odnoklassniki page. The District Court extended detention on 23 September, 26 October, 21 and 23 December 2022, finding continued risks of absconding and influencing witnesses, among others.

In January 2023 the investigation was completed and the case was sent to the Zhovtnevyi District Court of Kharkiv. From 25 January 2023 and approximately bi-monthly thereafter, the trial court extended detention on the same grounds. Appeals raised the absence of reasonable suspicion and risks, the fact that delay was not attributable to the applicants, unchanged reasons, and lack of effective scrutiny; they argued that the Exceptions to Mandatory Bail Clause allowed but did not require denial of bail, cited domestic cases where bail had been set, and referred to Piruzyan v. Armenia. The Court of Appeal upheld the extensions. Some orders referred to the Wartime Detention Clause and/or the Exceptions to Mandatory Bail Clause.

In October 2022 new charges were added against the second applicant under Article 436-2 § 2 of the Criminal Code for publishing material justifying Russian aggression on the Russian social network between March and June 2022. The most recent detention extension orders were dated 13 December 2024. There is no information on further progress in the proceedings. In a domestic constitutional decision of 19 June 2024, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine declared the Wartime Detention Clause constitutional and stated that it did not mandate detention without alternatives and that courts could still set bail.
001-251252:
First applicant Anatoliy Ivanovych Derevyanko and second applicant Yuliya Mykolayivna Tarasova, Ukrainian nationals, lodged applications concerning pre-trial detention for national-security offences. Derevyanko worked as an engineer at a private grain-processing and mill factory in Balakliya, occupied by Russian forces in March 2022 and retaken in September 2022. On 29 November 2022 criminal proceedings began over alleged collaborationist activity under Article 111-1 §4. On 10 March 2023 he was notified of suspicion, arrested and questioned. The prosecution alleged that from 1 August 2022, as acting manager, he coordinated factory activities, held staff meetings, distributed work, received reports, attended occupation-administration meetings, sought salaries and accepted grain for storage. The investigator sought detention, citing a less serious offence (3–5 years), cooperation with Russian authorities, flight risk to Russia and witness influence. On 14 March 2023 the Novomoskovskyi District Court ordered pre-trial detention, relying on the Wartime Detention Clause and Exceptions to Mandatory Bail Clause and finding risks of absconding and influencing witnesses. He opposed, arguing no evidence of risk, a less serious offence, that he had stayed after liberation, that witnesses had evacuated, his family ties, age 56 and no criminal record. He argued that automatic bail denial was contrary to Article 5 §3, that reasons were repetitive and that there was no reasonable suspicion. The case was sent to trial on 29 April 2023. From 8 May 2023 to 2 October 2024 the trial court repeatedly rejected release and extended detention, finding the risks undiminished. The Kharkiv Court of Appeal upheld those decisions, citing public-interest and social-values reasoning; on 30 July 2024 it also cited reoffending risk. Witnesses were questioned from 22 August 2023 to 6 February 2024. On 30 October 2024 he was convicted and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment, suspended for three years, with a position ban. On 19 December 2024 the appeal court upheld the conviction but replaced imprisonment with a UAH 170,000 fine and asset confiscation. The Supreme Court was examining points-of-law appeals.

Second applicant Tarasova worked from December 2020 as a freelance sales representative for N., a Ukrainian medicines manufacturer. In March 2023 the SBU investigated assisting the aggressor State under Article 111-2 (10–12 years, optional confiscation). The alleged scheme involved N.’s management disguising anaesthetic shipments to Russia as shipments to an Estonian company via Vilnius, final destination Armenia, but diverted through Belarus to Russian company A. Medication allegedly found with a Russian prisoner of war was not part of the charges. In June 2023 the SBU searched N.’s premises; Tarasova was interviewed as a witness and provided phone messaging content. On 14 September 2023 she was notified of suspicion and questioned, accused of conspiracy and transmitting material resources to the aggressor State. The investigator sought detention, alleging flight risk, including to Russia, financial resources, destruction of WhatsApp/electronic evidence and influencing employees, witnesses and co-conspirators. She opposed, arguing no evidence of intent or risks; she was married with two minor children; she had known of the investigation since late June 2023, cooperated and not absconded; border crossings with Russia were closed; she had voluntarily shared her phone; other suspects had been charged earlier; and she was not management, so no reoffending risk. On 20 September 2023 the Shevchenkivskyi District Court of Kyiv ordered detention, citing reasonable suspicion, punishment, witness/evidence risks, dangerousness and grounds not to set bail. The Kyiv Court of Appeal upheld it on 4 October 2023, adding continuing-offence risk and the Wartime Detention Clause. On 15 November 2023 the District Court extended detention, finding risks of absconding, influencing witnesses, destroying evidence and reoffending; further extensions about every two months were upheld on similar grounds. On 25 June 2024 bail was set, paid, and she was released.

Filipe de Jesus Pinhal, born in 1946, was a member of Banco Comercial Português (“BCP”) board from 1994, vice-chairman from 1998, and chairman of its executive committee from August 2007. From 1999 to 2007, BCP allegedly operated a “circular trading” scheme through offshore companies—17 in the Cayman Islands, four in the Isle of Man, British Virgin Islands and Gibraltar, and a real-estate group—financed by BCP loans to buy and sell BCP shares and influence their market price. The scheme allegedly caused nearly EUR 590 million in losses, which BCP allegedly concealed in its accounts. In November–December 2007, shareholder J.B. complained to the CMVM, the Banco de Portugal (“BdP”) and the Attorney General. Criminal, CMVM and BdP proceedings followed, with information exchanged among them.

In the BdP proceedings, opened on 26 December 2007 against BCP and ten individuals, the applicant was interviewed on 16 April 2008. On 11 December 2008 the BdP accused him of three counts of reporting false or incomplete information to the BdP from 2000 to 2007 and six counts of false accounting. By decision of 27 April 2010, the BdP found him guilty of two reporting counts and four false-accounting counts. It imposed an overall fine of EUR 425,000 on the reporting counts and did not fine the false-accounting counts because he was already being prosecuted criminally for forgery and use of forged documents. It also imposed publication of the sanction and a seven-year disqualification. The applicant challenged this before the Lisbon Local Criminal Court on 16 July 2010, alleging inter alia a breach of ne bis in idem. On 29 August 2014 that court dismissed the complaint and upheld the sanctions. On 9 June 2015 the Lisbon Court of Appeal held parts of the reporting prosecution time-barred, acquitted him of the remaining counts concerning the E.A. group, and the judgment became final on 26 June 2015.

In the criminal proceedings, the public prosecutor opened an investigation on 21 December 2007 for market manipulation, forgery and use of forged documents, and aggravated fraud. The applicant was interviewed on 13 April 2009. On 23 June 2009 the public prosecutor indicted him. On 27 July 2010 the investigation judge committed him for trial on market manipulation and forgery/use of forged documents, finding no case on aggravated fraud. On 2 May 2014 the Lisbon District Court convicted him of market manipulation, acquitted him of forgery/use of forged documents, and sentenced him to two years’ imprisonment suspended on payment of EUR 300,000 to charity, plus a four-year ban. On 25 February 2015 the Lisbon Court of Appeal upheld the conviction and rejected his ne bis in idem argument, finding the offences and protected legal interests different. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal on 12 November 2015 and upheld that decision on 4 May 2016. The criminal conviction became final on 14 July 2016. Later applications to dismiss the criminal proceedings after the BdP acquittal were rejected on 14 and 21 October 2016; his prison sentence was declared terminated on 6 November 2018.

In the CMVM proceedings, the CMVM opened supervisory proceedings on 7 December 2007 and administrative proceedings on 29 December 2008 against BCP board members, including the applicant. It accused him of six counts of failure to provide quality information concerning false or incomplete accounting reports for 2003–2006, a third-quarter 2007 report, and a statement of 23 December 2007. On 9 July 2010 the CMVM found him guilty on six counts, imposed an EUR 800,000 fine, a five-year professional ban and a five-year disqualification. The Lisbon Local Criminal Court upheld this on 18 January 2013. On 6 March 2014 the Lisbon Court of Appeal found two counts time-barred, reduced the fine to EUR 700,000 on four counts, and reduced the ancillary sanctions to two years and six months. It did not address ne bis in idem. The Constitutional Court declared an appeal inadmissible on 27 March 2015. On 23 October 2015 the Lisbon Local Criminal Court found one further count time-barred and adjourned reassessment of the overall sanction. On 4 April 2018 the applicant again alleged ne bis in idem before that court, referring to the BdP acquittal and criminal conviction, and sought a CJEU preliminary ruling. On 8 June 2018 the court noted the final decisions and found ne bis in idem not applicable to calculation of the overall administrative fine.

The applicant lodged applications with the Court on 24 September 2015 and 3 January 2020. He alleged that he had been prosecuted and tried three times for the same acts by the criminal authorities, the CMVM and the BdP, and that no effective domestic remedy existed. He also raised complaints under Articles 6 and 7 in the second application.

The applications were brought against Azerbaijan by three Azerbaijani nationals, all resident in Baku: Ali Farzulla oglu Alishov (born 1956), Adil Fatulla oglu Huseynov (born 1966), and Bahman Tapdig oglu Abbasov (born 1950). They were represented by Javad Javadov, a lawyer based in Azerbaijan. Their applications were lodged on 21 June 2023 (Alishov, application no. 25527/23), 21 June 2023 (Huseynov, application no. 25578/23), and 22 September 2023 (Abbasov, application no. 36156/23).

On different dates in 2015, separate and unrelated criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicants under Article 178.3.2 of the Criminal Code of Azerbaijan, concerning fraud causing large-scale damage. On 15 May 2015, the Narimanov District Court remanded the second applicant, Huseynov, in custody. On 3 November 2015, the same court remanded the first applicant, Alishov, in custody. On 25 May 2015, the third applicant, Abbasov, was placed under police supervision as a preventive measure.

On 30 May 2016, the second applicant was released from detention, and the preventive measure of placing him under police supervision was applied. On 21 October 2016, the first applicant was likewise released from detention, and the same preventive measure was applied to him. From that point onward, according to the record, no investigative actions were carried out in the proceedings against the applicants.

In 2023, the applicants lodged complaints with the ordinary courts under the procedure for reviewing the lawfulness of procedural actions or decisions by investigating authorities. They complained about the length of the criminal proceedings against them and sought discontinuation of the preventive measure placing them under police supervision. That measure, according to the applicants, effectively prevented them from leaving Azerbaijan.

By final domestic decisions of 5 June 2023 in respect of the first and second applicants, and of 14 September 2023 in respect of the third applicant, the Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ complaints. The Court of Appeal held that there had been no unlawful procedural actions or decisions by the investigating authorities.

The applicants complained before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the excessive length of the criminal proceedings. They also complained under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention about the preventive measure placing them under police supervision, which had prevented them from leaving Azerbaijan.

The case concerns three applications lodged against Ukraine: Oleg Vasylyovych Shytikov, Galyna Yuriyivna Fomina, and Valeriy Viktorovych Vasylenko. The applications were introduced on 17 June 2025 (no. 19489/25), 25 August 2025 (no. 27348/25), and 25 August 2025 (no. 28828/25), respectively. Ms Fomina was represented before the Court by Anastasiya Leonidivna Lutkovska-Babych, based in Kyiv. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications.

The applicants complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. The factual details supplied are contained in the appended table.

Mr Shytikov, born in 1961, stated that the civil proceedings at issue began on 24 March 2017. As recorded in the table, those proceedings were still pending at the time of the application. The total length was more than nine years, two months and twenty-three days, and the proceedings involved three levels of jurisdiction.

Ms Fomina, born in 1995, stated that the civil proceedings began on 25 November 2020. Those proceedings were also recorded as pending. The total length was more than five years, six months and twenty-two days, involving two levels of jurisdiction.

Mr Vasylenko, born in 1980, is recorded in the appended table as having start dates of 19 August 2020 and 11 April 2024, and end dates of 21 December 2021 and pending. The table records a total length of more than three years, six months and fourteen days, with one level of jurisdiction.

Beyond these dates, lengths, jurisdictional levels, and the applicants’ complaints, the supplied factual record contains no concrete descriptions of the underlying civil disputes, no details of the domestic courts’ decisions or reasoning, and no account of specific procedural steps taken in the domestic proceedings. It also does not identify the opposing parties in the domestic civil cases, the subject matter of those cases, or the particular domestic remedies the applicants may have used or attempted to use. The record states only that the applicants alleged that the civil proceedings were excessively long and that no effective domestic remedy was available for that complaint.

D.T., a Greek national born in 1984, suffers from bipolar disorder and drug addiction. Medical records show he was hospitalised in 2007 at Aiginiteio public hospital for bipolar psychosis, hospitalised for several weeks in 2012 at Dromokaiteio Psychiatric Hospital for bipolar disorder, and in 2015 certified as 67% disabled due to bipolar disorder, having been hospitalised at least twice and receiving medication (Depakine Chrono, Akineton, Aloperidin, Invega). He received disability benefits.

On 4 December 2020 he was charged with joining a criminal organisation and drug trafficking and detained at Korydallos Prison Psychiatric Hospital under order no. 148/2020 of the Athens Investigating Judge. On 17 December 2020, a court-appointed psychiatrist found him a drug addict (cocaine, stimulant pills) with underlying bipolar emotional psychosis (F31), requiring special therapeutic care. On 22 December 2020, his treating psychiatrist at Dromokaiteio stated he had treated him since 2012, that he had twice been involuntarily hospitalised for bipolar disorder, and that his chronic serious psychiatric disorder required medication without fail, regular psychiatric monitoring and avoidance of cannabis.

In May 2021, in proceedings on prolongation of pre-trial detention, D.T. argued that detention was incompatible with his health because regular psychiatric monitoring would be impossible. He said he had taken medication without fail and had not used drugs for eight months; if released, he would live with his mother and enter rehabilitation. On 7 June 2021, the Indictment Division of the Athens Court of Misdemeanours extended detention until 27 November 2021 (order no. 1987/2021), citing reasonable suspicion of repeated, organised felonies carrying possible life imprisonment, sometimes committed in schools, and finding restrictive measures insufficient. On 6 July 2021, the Athens Investigating Judge dismissed his request to lift detention (order no. 198/2021), noting the psychiatric report but stating that under Article 30 of Law no. 4139/2013 drug addicts were not entitled to favourable treatment for the offence, so there were no grounds to assess the report further. Order no. 1476/2021 of the Indictment Division of the Athens Criminal Court of Appeal extended detention until 27 May 2022. On 14 April 2022, the Athens Criminal Court of Appeal acquitted him of joining a criminal organisation but convicted him of drug trafficking as a drug addict, imposing a four-year sentence suspended pending appeal. He appealed and was released on 18 April 2022.

As to medical care, he was held at Korydallos Prison Psychiatric Hospital from 4 to 11 December 2020, Amfissa Prison from 11 December 2020 to 19 March 2021, and Korydallos Prison from 19 March 2021 until 18 April 2022. A 23 January 2023 prison deputy director report stated he was examined by prison psychiatrists on 4 December 2020 and 18 February 2022 and by an independent expert on 5 December 2020; on 18 February 2022 he reported not taking medication regularly and one pill was added; he received prescribed medication, had pharmacy access, and made no complaints; the deputy concluded treatment was adequate. His file recorded bipolar disorder and prescriptions: a 7 December 2020 discharge note (Depakine Chrono 500 mg twice nightly, Nozinan 25 mg, Akineton 2 mg, Aloperidin 10 mg, Invega 9 mg), an 11 December 2020 Amfissa doctor’s card adding Nozinan 25 mg half tablet nightly, and an 18 February 2022 note that he did not wish to take Stedon 10 at night. Other entries concerned dermatitis, knee problems and a burnt finger.

Domestic law included Penal Code provisions on complaints, prison council, healthcare and hospitalisation; Code of Criminal Procedure provisions on appealing pre-trial detention and prosecutorial supervision; Ministerial Decision no. 58819/2003; and Law no. 4139/2013 on treatment of drug users. Domestic case-law (Supreme Administrative Court judgment no. 582/2021; Court of Cassation judgment no. 1684/1998) addressed jurisdiction over execution-of-sentence complaints. A CPT report of 2 September 2022 on a November-December 2021 visit noted no single comprehensive multidisciplinary medical record at Korydallos Prison Special Health Centre, separate doctor/nurse journals, no individual care plan, brief entries, and recommended a single computerised health record and individual care plan. D.T. lodged an application with the Court on 15 October 2021, complaining under Articles 3 and 13 about inadequate psychiatric monitoring and medication in detention and lack of an effective remedy.

The case concerns Romels Tovmasyan’s complaint about the investigation into the death of his daughter, M. Guloyan. The applicant is an Armenian national born in 1945, living in Byureghavan. His daughter married G.G. in 2009; they had a child and lived in the same house as G.G.’s parents, brother, uncle and the uncle’s family. On 12 July 2012 M. Guloyan asked her brother, M.T., to visit and told him she wanted a divorce, since she and G.G. frequently fought over his unemployment and gambling. They agreed M.T. would return that evening with their parents.

At 8.50 p.m. that day the Kotayk Regional Police received a report from Abovyan Medical Centre that M. Guloyan had died. Hospital records showed admission at 7.20 p.m.; a 9 p.m. register entry recorded a dead body brought in with injuries of criminal origin. Police opened a criminal investigation into her death and ordered an autopsy. A.G., the wife of G.G.’s uncle, stated that around 7 p.m., after finding M. Guloyan’s one-year-old alone, she saw M. Guloyan hanging by a cloth from a metal pole in the bathroom. She cut the rope with a knife, took the body down, called for help, and she and her husband took M. Guloyan to hospital, where she was pronounced dead. A photojournalist later attended the funeral and photographed visible injuries, including a neck bruise and wounds and bruises on the hands.

On 16 August 2012 forensic expert A.M. issued the autopsy report, without attaching photographs. It found death from unnatural causes; a ligature mark from a firm object possibly a bathrobe belt; bruises on the front of the neck; a scratch on the right side; no objective signs of other injuries apart from those; subclinical alcohol intoxication; and that she was 7–8 weeks pregnant. After the funeral photographs were provided, a forensic technical examination on 12 November 2012 confirmed they had not been manipulated. On 23 November 2012 an additional forensic medical examination by exhumation was ordered; its 25 December 2012 report listed the same injuries and said other pictured injuries could have remained undiscovered due to decomposition. On 28 December 2012 an expert commission including psychiatrist V.B. found no mental disorder but possible depression and doubted suicide.

In January 2013 A.G. changed her account of the discovery; G.G.’s father suggested “genetic problems” contributed to suicide. In March 2013 V.B. said there was no scientifically proven answer on genetic cause. At a reconstruction, A.G. could not cut the noose while holding a dummy without it falling, then stated she had not taken the body down but knelt and the body fell on her.

On 22 April 2013 the investigation was terminated for absence of corpus delicti, finding suicide due to depression over the divorce. The applicant appealed; on 24 June 2013 the Prosecutor General’s Office set the decision aside, citing missing neck/hand injuries in the autopsy, absent autopsy photographs, and contradictions about the time of discovery and transfer. The investigation resumed and was transferred to the Nor Nork Investigative Department in Yerevan. Further witnesses, including G.G., A.M. and hospital staff, were questioned. G.G. said his wife never consumed alcohol; A.M. said he noticed no other injuries and had thrown away spoiled film.

On 20 November 2013 Nor Nork terminated the investigation for lack of evidence of a crime, relying on denials of injuries, the autopsy, A.M.’s statement, medical staff, the psychiatric assessment, the half-brothers’ suicides, and V.B. not ruling out suicide. It found the body was admitted at 7.20 p.m., resuscitation was performed, and death was pronounced at 9 p.m. The applicant unsuccessfully appealed to the prosecutor, then sought judicial review, challenging the expert reports, lack of access to material, unanswered contradictions, alcohol evidence, and absence of cross-examinations. On 18 March 2014 the District Court upheld the termination; the Court of Appeal upheld that decision; and on 2 July 2014, served on 16 July 2014, the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on points of law.

I.W., a Polish national born in 1972 and living in Gdynia, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 17 March 2021. The underlying events concerned her civil action against her former employer.

In December 2019 the applicant lodged a civil action against her former employer, seeking PLN 250,000 (approximately EUR 58,700) in compensation and an apology for damage allegedly caused by harassment in the workplace, which she claimed to have suffered for four years, and her resulting inability to work. She applied for legal aid and for exemption from the applicable court fee of PLN 12,500 (approximately EUR 3,000). In support, she submitted a declaration of means showing that she had no income and debts amounting to approximately PLN 70,000 (approximately EUR 16,400), together with certificates confirming that she was unemployed and ineligible for unemployment benefits.

On 5 February 2020 the Gdańsk Regional Court ordered the applicant to provide additional information. It asked, among other things, whether she had already received PLN 45,000 (approximately EUR 10,600) awarded to her in separate proceedings against the former employer. The applicant replied that she was receiving a monthly stipend of PLN 700 (approximately EUR 165) from her studies, occasional private loans, and support from her parents and her son. She confirmed that in March 2019 she had received the award mentioned by the Regional Court, but said she had already spent it to repay part of her debts.

On 5 April 2020 the Regional Court dismissed the applications for legal aid and exemption from court fees. It considered that the applicant had failed to provide exhaustive information. It noted that she had declared no income, whereas her expenses—excluding, among other things, food and clothing—amounted to approximately PLN 1,050 (approximately EUR 250) per month, and there was no reasonable explanation of how those expenses had been covered. The Regional Court was not convinced that the applicant and her husband lived only on loans, which were also not indicated in her declaration, given by her parents. It also held that the applicant had sufficient qualifications to find employment and that she had failed to explain why her allegedly ill husband had not applied for incapacity benefits. It further noted that she had informed it of the stipend only after the request for additional information and concluded that she might have failed to disclose other sources of income. As regards the previous award, the Regional Court considered that the applicant should have saved part of it and stated that the State Treasury could not assume the obligation to pay court fees for those who had decided to improve their standard of living by taking out loans.

The applicant appealed, arguing that she had no regular income. She added that only recently the local social welfare authority had granted her and her husband a social assistance benefit (zasiłek stały) and food assistance, amounting to a total of PLN 728 (approximately EUR 170) per month.

On 28 August 2020 the Regional Court dismissed the appeal, stating that despite her difficult situation, the applicant could afford to pay the fee. It held that the most important factor was her failure to save part of the previous award. While acknowledging that she had been granted benefits addressed to those unable to work, it raised doubts as to why she and her husband had not applied for other benefits financed by social insurance.

On 23 November 2020 the Regional Court returned the applicant’s claim as unpaid.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the dismissal of her application for an exemption from the court fee had resulted in a disproportionate restriction of her right of access to court, as guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
001-252039:
A.S., a Latvian national born in 1957 living in Cēsis, complains that Latvia failed in its positive obligations under Article 4 in response to her allegations that she was subjected to servitude or forced labour on dairy farm M in Cēsis parish. The events concern two workers: G.R. and later A.S., between September 2016 and May 2017. Farm owner company E, represented by M.Z., rented the premises to company K.A., represented by D.G.

In August 2016 G.R. answered D.G.’s job advertisement. They orally agreed that G.R. would learn dairy machinery and receive EUR 5 per day initially, later EUR 15 per day; no written contract was signed. G.R. later stayed in the utility annex. He complained of health problems, and D.G. bought medicines. G.R. left at the end of September 2016 after a payment dispute.

In December 2016 A.S. saw the advertisement and contacted D.G. They discussed work and accommodation; D.G. suggested renting nearby. On 20 December 2016 A.S. arrived with her belongings and insisted on staying. D.G. installed stoves. No written contract was signed. A.S. performed two milking sessions daily and operated and cleaned dairy equipment. She asked D.G. to buy groceries, cigarettes and phone cards. After the dairy company reported reduced milk quality, D.G. disposed of milk or compensated losses. A.S. asked about salary; D.G. said dairy payments were withheld. In April 2017 D.G. gave her EUR 50 to see a doctor; she left to visit her sister but returned because her belongings remained. On 4 May 2017 D.G. removed livestock and equipment and moved out; on 9 May 2017 he told M.Z. the rent had ended. A.S. stayed and assisted M.Z. In May 2017, on M.Z.’s suggestion, she complained to the State Labour Inspectorate about unpaid salary. The SLI forwarded the complaint to police, D.G. did not reply, K.A. was fined, and the SLI advised civil labour litigation.

On 26 May 2017 the police opened criminal proceedings under Section 154¹ of the Criminal Law concerning trafficking. An on-site examination found a utility annex with water, electricity, insulated windows, furniture, appliances, stoves and a shower/WC. A.S. was declared a victim and received State-funded rehabilitation and social services. Witnesses included M.Z., a food/veterinary official, former worker A.B., G.R., dairy employees and D.G.’s acquaintances. G.R. said he stayed voluntarily to save money and left after unpaid wages. A.S. testified she responded because she was unemployed, negotiated orally, milked cows, maintained phone contact with her sister, and never went hungry. In January 2018 she received EUR 1,330 in State victim compensation. D.G. was charged in August 2018 and indicted in October 2018.

On 20 September 2019 the Vidzeme District Court convicted D.G. of trafficking, sentenced him to two years’ imprisonment suspended for two years, and ordered compensation. It found the victims elderly and health-affected, dependent on promises of payment, exploited, and reinforced in vulnerability by food provision. On 9 March 2020 the Vidzeme Regional Court quashed the judgment and acquitted D.G., finding no “accommodation” for trafficking, no forced labour, insufficient vulnerability and no intent; the parties acted in an employment relationship and could leave. On 31 March 2021 the Supreme Court Senate quashed the acquittal and remitted the case, criticising the vulnerability analysis, the treatment of registered domiciles, D.G.’s awareness of worsening conditions, his lack of objection to accommodation, repeated salary promises, and the victims’ lack of other income. On 22 March 2022 the Regional Court again acquitted D.G., finding no accommodation intention, work not excessive, no vulnerability, no forced labour/servitude and no intent; it rejected a psychologist’s opinion as influenced and found A.S. understood the circumstances. On 25 October 2022 the Supreme Court refused to initiate cassation proceedings, finding the appellate court had examined the evidence and no grounds existed.
001-252041:
The application was lodged by Mr Anestis Spyridonidis, a Greek national born in 1984 living in Xanthi, against Armenia. He was represented by lawyers A. Ghazaryan and A. Dashyan. The Armenian Government was represented initially by L. Drmeyan and subsequently by K. Andreasyan. The application concerned the domestic courts’ refusal to order the return of the applicant’s children to their habitual place of residence in Greece under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, and the length of the return proceedings.

In 2012 the applicant married his former wife, S.S., in Ukraine. Their older son, S.Sp., was born in Greece in 2013. It appears that in 2014 the family moved to Ukraine, where their younger son, M.Sp., was born in 2020. Both children are Greek nationals. In 2022, because of the war in Ukraine, the family returned to Greece. The applicant arranged for S.Sp. to receive private Greek language training with a view to enrolling him in the first grade the following school year. On 11 July 2022 the family travelled from Greece to Armenia. The applicant submitted that it had been agreed they would return to Greece shortly afterwards, but in December 2022 S.S. refused to do so.

On 26 April 2023 the applicant initiated judicial proceedings seeking the children’s return to Greece under the Hague Convention. On 12 June 2023 S.Sp. was heard by the judge at a court hearing, in the absence of his parents and in the presence of their representatives and a psychologist. He opposed returning to Greece, stating among other things that he did not speak Greek and did not have friends in Greece, unlike in Armenia where he attended school.

On 6 July 2023 the Kotayk Regional Court dismissed the application. It found that the retention was wrongful within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention, because both parents had joint custody and the children’s habitual residence was Greece. However, relying on Article 13 §§ 1(b) and 2 of the Hague Convention, the court held that the children’s return to Greece would expose them to a grave risk of psychological harm and would place them in an intolerable situation. The court relied on several pieces of evidence: a psychologist’s opinion from the custody and guardianship body stating that S.Sp. felt safer and closer emotionally to his mother and more comfortable in Armenia owing to his Armenian language skills and social ties; S.Sp.’s clear objection, with the court finding he had sufficient maturity and no evidence that his views had been influenced or directed by S.S.; an expert report by a psychological centre submitted by S.S. stating that S.Sp. felt safe with his mother and brother, rejected residing with the applicant, and would suffer serious psychological stress if separated from his mother, and that he had been traumatised by war scenes in Ukraine and parental conflicts, giving rise to fears of separation and harm to his mother; the children’s short period in Greece, lack of Greek, and incomplete integration there, whereas S.Sp. was fully integrated in Armenia and fluent in Armenian; and the court’s view that, given his vulnerable emotional state, return would expose him to further psychological trauma. As regards M.Sp., the court concluded that, given his young age, having lived with his mother and brother since birth, and the importance of maintaining the sibling bond, it was in his best interests to remain in Armenia.

On 20 July 2023 the applicant lodged an appeal, complaining among other things about the use of the psychological centre’s report, which he said had been obtained without his participation or knowledge. On 13 February 2024 the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. On 23 May 2024 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. On 17 July 2024 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible for lack of merit. The application to the European Court of Human Rights was lodged on 29 November 2024.
