The complaint concerns the Dutch authorities’ refusal of residence permits for five minor children of the applicant, A.A., a Yemeni national born in 1970 and living in Helvoirt. He had contracted polygamous marriages in Yemen with three women and had thirteen children: eight with his first wife, three with his second, and two with his third.

On 17 October 2018 the applicant entered the Netherlands and applied for a temporary asylum residence permit. It was granted on 12 July 2019, valid from 23 October 2018 to 23 October 2023. On 20 November 2023 he received a permanent asylum residence permit valid from 23 October 2023.

On 25 July 2019, while his family members were in Türkiye, the applicant applied for family reunification for his first wife and all thirteen children. On 30 August 2019 the Immigration and Naturalisation Service (IND) informed him that polygamy was contrary to Dutch public order and asked him to choose one marriage for recognition under Dutch law; only that wife and her children would be eligible. On 16 September 2019 the applicant said he wished to maintain the application for his first wife and the children from all three marriages. The authorities treated this as his having chosen the first marriage.

On 27 December 2019 the IND granted reunification for the first wife and their eight children, but refused it for the five children born of the second and third marriages (R., Ra., W., N. and A.). It relied on Article 4(4) of the Family Reunification Directive, as implemented in section 3.16 of the Aliens Decree 2000, which contains a polygamy exception.

On 21 January 2020 the applicant objected, submitting grounds on 21 February 2020. He argued that polygamy was not automatically contrary to public order and that an individual assessment was required. He cited severe consequences of divorce for his second and third wives, including social stigma and discrimination; his children’s disadvantaged situation in Türkiye with temporary kimlik documents and limited access to services; and the impossibility of returning to Yemen because of a real risk of ill-treatment linked to his and the mothers’ human-rights activities. The IND asked on 10 June 2020 whether divorce was possible. In replies of 1 and 30 July 2020, the applicant said he could not contact the Yemeni authorities and that divorce would harm his wives. A hearing was conducted in writing because of COVID-19. He later submitted evidence of financial support, threats, mothers’ declarations consenting to the children living with him, and translations of further threat evidence.

On 21 January 2021 the IND rejected the objection as manifestly ill-founded and maintained the refusal. It considered that the applicant was bound by one recognised marriage; only one wife and her minor children were eligible. It stressed that polygamy was contrary to Dutch public order. It found the children were not in dire circumstances in Türkiye because they lived with their biological mothers, had kimlik documents, and had access to services, housing, schools and private clinics. It noted the applicant had not cared for them since leaving Yemen, could maintain contact and visit them, and had visited in March 2020. It found no compelling interests.

On 19 March 2021 the applicant sought judicial review. He argued he sought reunification only with the children, with the mothers’ consent, not with the second and third wives; that polygamy was not automatically contrary to public order; that divorce and Yemen-related risks should be considered; and that insufficient weight was given to the children’s interests. He submitted a 28 May 2019 psychometric report for R.

On 21 September 2021 the District Court of The Hague, sitting in Amsterdam, declared the review unfounded. It found the IND had wrongly called the objection manifestly ill-founded but treated this as a clerical error. It held that denial was in principle authorised but required an individualised assessment; that asylum-related risks belonged to asylum proceedings; that the children were not in dire circumstances; and that the psychometric report was insufficient.

On 19 October 2021 the applicant appealed to the Administrative Jurisdiction Division, supplementing his appeal on 25 November 2021 and 2 February 2022. He added arguments about changing Dutch views on family structures and polyamory, asylum-related family problems, and the children’s best interests. On 13 October 2022 the Division upheld the dismissal. It reasoned that polygamy was contrary to Dutch public order and public morality, that changing views did not alter this, and that the State Secretary had made an individualised assessment and could attach great weight to the polygamous situation. The rejection became final. Later, the second wife was granted asylum on 24 June 2025, and on 18 July 2025 she applied for family reunification for her children; that application was pending.
001-252193:
The case concerns an application lodged against Georgia by Ms Irine Nadashvili, a Georgian national born in 1980 who lives in Gurjaani. She was represented by Ms N. Londaridze. The Georgian Government were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Dzamashvili. The application, no. 31727/23, was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 8 August 2023. According to the record, its subject matter is the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings pending before a court of first instance since April 2021.

On 9 August 2020, after returning from Türkiye to Georgia, the applicant was placed in quarantine in a designated hotel as a COVID-19 measure. On 10 August 2020, in view of her alleged refusal to undergo a nasal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test, she was transferred by the police to a psychiatric hospital. The applicant alleged that, while in hospital, she had been confined to a single room, deprived of her personal belongings, including her mobile phone, and prevented from communicating with the outside world. She further alleged that she had been forcibly subjected to a nasal PCR test and compelled to take certain psychotropic medication.

After lodging multiple complaints with, among others, the police and the hospital, on 12 April 2021 the applicant lodged a civil complaint against the Ministry of Health and Social Protection. She requested compensation for what she described as unlawful detention and inhuman and degrading treatment at the psychiatric facility. She also made two procedural applications: first, that the Batumi City Court order the retrieval of relevant video footage from the psychiatric hospital; and second, that it obtain information concerning written communications between various public health authorities regarding arrangements for her isolation following her return from Türkiye.

On 19 April 2021, the applicant was informed by telephone that her civil claim had been admitted for examination. On the same date, the Batumi City Court granted her application concerning retrieval of the video evidence and rejected the other application. On 29 April 2021, the court was informed that the recordings had not been archived and were therefore inaccessible. On 27 May 2021, the Ministry submitted its position in reply to the applicant’s claim. On 20 July 2021, the applicant made another application requesting the examination of several witnesses in court.

Following the transfer of the judge assigned to the case to another court, the case was assigned to a new judge on 17 March 2022. On 28 March 2022, it was reassigned yet again. On 17 November 2025, the judge responsible for examining the case scheduled a preparatory hearing for 23 February 2026. According to the case file, the civil proceedings remained pending before the Batumi City Court at the time covered by the record.

The applicant, Pertch Margaryan, an Armenian national born in 1963, lives in Gyumri. His son, A. Margaryan, was conscripted in December 2013 and assigned to military unit no. 38636 of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces in Shushi. Service records from December 2013, February 2014 and July 2014 described him as psychologically stable, positive about service and without adaptation problems. In July 2014 he was transferred to another division near Hadrut.

On 4 December 2014 A. Margaryan was found in a trench next to sentry post no. 1 with a gunshot wound to his chest. At 3.50 p.m. the Investigative Committee was informed that he had shot himself and died. Investigator S.H. opened criminal proceedings under Article 110 of the 2003 Criminal Code (incitement to suicide). The scene examination recovered an AKMS rifle, magazines, ammunition, clothing, a knife, a Bible, a mirror and a wooden cross. An internal investigation report of 8 December 2014 stated that A. Margaryan had taken up duty around 3.10 p.m.; Private M.A. later saw him lying in the trench, believed he was asleep and did not tell Captain G.K.; M.A. and Junior Sergeant H.A. then found blood and called for help. The report noted that nobody heard the gunshot, no traces of violence were found, and A. Margaryan wore thermal rather than ordinary underwear. It could not clarify the reasons for death, any link to religious convictions, Captain G.K.’s failure to notice his absence, or the underwear issue.

Witnesses described A. Margaryan variously as modest, reserved, unsociable and responsible. Private M.M. heard a sound like a gunshot around 3.40 p.m. Captain G.K. said he had formed the impression that A. Margaryan shot himself but could not say with certainty what happened. Private A.H. stated that A. Margaryan had felt down because someone called “Aleksan” had been convicted because of him, and later said nobody would socialise with him at school. A.A. (Aleksan) had been given a suspended sentence on 6 November 2014 in a case in which A. Margaryan had testified as a key witness. Operational police checks in 2015 sought information about possible threats, contact by A.A., or rumours in the unit; no such information was obtained, but A.H. reported A. Margaryan’s regret after testifying.

Forensic reports found death from a penetrating chest wound, with a trajectory from front to back, left to right and downward. Ballistic examination found no identifiable fingerprints on the rifle, although the cartridge matched the weapon; copper particulates were found on swabs from Private A.V. A reconstruction showed shots could be heard from sentry post no. 4. A posthumous psychological and psychiatric report of 28 December 2015 concluded that A. Margaryan had no mental illness but had schizoid personality traits and maladjustment, and had killed himself.

On 4 February 2016 investigator D.N. terminated the criminal investigation, finding that the death was not the result of an unlawful act but self-inflicted due to psychological traits. The applicant appealed to the prosecutor, arguing that the investigation had not properly examined possible retaliation for his son’s testimony, the absence of a bullet, lack of fingerprints on the weapon, absence of gunshot residue on his hands, failure to take swabs from all servicemen, unclear circumstances of discovery and transfer, and identical witness statements. The military prosecutor dismissed the appeal on 30 April 2016. The First Instance Court of General Jurisdiction of Syunik Region dismissed the applicant’s judicial review claim on 23 August 2016, finding a complete and objective investigation. The Criminal Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 2 November 2016, and the Court of Cassation refused leave to appeal on 31 January 2017.
001-252384:
The case involves two applications against Serbia lodged by Serbian nationals. Application no. 34317/17 was brought by Milan Đorđević, born in 1970, residing in Odžaci, represented by Branislav Milojičić, and lodged on 13 April 2017. Application no. 75858/17 was brought by Saša Milosavljević, born in 1965, residing in Pančevo, represented by Branislav Manić, and lodged on 20 October 2017. The Serbian Government was represented by its Agent, Z. Jadrijević Mladar.

The subject matter concerns divergent domestic case-law on dismissal of police officers’ compensation claims for unpaid salary supplements for work on public holidays, night work and overtime (“work during unsociable hours”). From June 2013 onward, domestic courts both upheld and dismissed claims lodged by many colleagues of the applicants. Courts interpreted Article 147 §§ 1 and 3 of the Police Act differently and selected different comparator employees when assessing whether the claimants’ salary coefficients had been increased for work during unsociable hours. This led to conflicting decisions in factually identical claims. On 10 November 2015, seeking to harmonise lower-court case-law, the Supreme Court adopted a guiding legal opinion. It stated that a “comparable worker” had to be an authorised officer, rather than a civilian officer, with the same level of education as the claimant but who did not work during unsociable hours. Applying that method, lower courts subsequently allowed similar claims. Where courts continued to rule contrary to the legal opinion, the Supreme Court quashed the decisions and ordered retrials, or reversed appellate decisions following appeals on points of law.

As regards the applicants, on 20 April and 10 September 2015 the competent first-instance courts dismissed their claims, comparing their salary coefficients with those of civilian officers who had not worked during unsociable hours. The competent courts of appeal upheld those decisions, which became final on 4 and 16 December 2015. The applicants lodged constitutional appeals against those decisions, complaining of case-law divergence and noting that certain courts had allowed identical claims brought by their colleagues. The first applicant submitted evidence of inconsistent case-law in which courts had ruled in favour of claimants by comparing their salary coefficients with those of authorised officers. The applicants also complained that the lower courts had applied substantive law arbitrarily.

On 8 December 2016 the Constitutional Court dismissed the first applicant’s constitutional appeal. Referring to its previous decision no. Už-3827/2012 of 12 December 2012, it held that he had relied on a comparison with cases in which compensation claims had been upheld on different grounds, rather than on a differing method of comparison of salary coefficients. 001-252385:
Ms Kalliopi Melliou, a Greek national born in 1958 living in Athens, lodged application no. 15807/19 against the Hellenic Republic on 8 March 2019. She was represented by I. Kourtovik. The Greek Government was represented by its Agent and delegates. The interregional NGO “CREW AGAINST TORTURE” was granted leave to intervene and submitted comments. The application concerns the applicant’s full strip-search following her transfer to the Attica General Police Directorate (GADA) for identification purposes.

On the evening of 27 February 2013, the applicant, a photojournalist involved in political activity, was walking home when she encountered four police officers of the “DELTA Team” rapid response unit patrolling the Exarcheia neighbourhood in Athens. She noted down their licence plate numbers, thinking that a violent incident or arbitrary police action had occurred. The officers spotted her, stopped her and asked for identification. She asked them to show their badges first. She was then transferred in a police car to the Security Directorate of the GADA, on the sixth floor, for identification purposes.

At the Security Directorate, her mobile phone was taken, and she was asked to hand over her identity card, answer questions about the incident and surrender the note containing the officers’ licence plate numbers. She was then informed that she would undergo a body search. The duty officer took her to his office and called a female police officer, ordering her to carry out a body search. In his instructions he used the phrase “do not inspect the anus or vagina, only inspect the bum cheeks and... you know...”. He then left the applicant alone with the female officer. The female officer ordered the applicant to remove all her clothes, including her underwear, and conducted a full strip-search by visually inspecting her. Afterwards the applicant dressed, got back her personal belongings, including her identity card and mobile phone, and was allowed to leave.

On 25 April 2013 the applicant submitted a criminal complaint. On 22 December 2014 a criminal investigation was opened against the head of the Security Directorate, the duty officer on the night in question and the officer who had conducted the full strip-search.

By judgment no. 19158/2015 of 30 April 2015, the Athens Criminal Court for misdemeanours acquitted the officer who had conducted the search and sentenced the head of the Security Directorate and the duty officer to a suspended three-year prison term for serious violation of the applicant’s dignity. It found that the applicant had presented her identity card upon arrival, had not been arrested or charged with a criminal offence, and that a simple pat-down would have sufficed. It considered the search unnecessary and carried out for the sole purpose of intimidating and punishing her. It relied on the duty officer’s insulting and degrading loud instructions, which had frightened the applicant, and found that the full strip-search took place in a brightly lit office with a window facing the street and the blinds open, so that those inside were visible from outside.

The two police officers appealed. By judgments nos. 5465a/2017, 6041a/2017 and 256/2018 of 15 January 2018, the Athens Criminal Court of Appeal found that the applicant had provided her identification details and the note only when informed that she would be prosecuted under the flagrante delicto procedure for false unsworn testimony; that there were serious suspicions she had been involved in preparing terrorism; and that it was necessary to verify whether she carried sharp objects, pills or other items because she had entered the building without passing through a body scanner or metal detector. It held the full strip-search necessary as a preventive measure. It found the search took place in a closed office, before a single female officer, without physical contact, with blinds closed and no established visibility from outside. It lasted about five minutes, involved no physical or verbal violence and did not infringe her dignity. It found the duty officer’s instruction constituted the offence of insult, but discontinued his prosecution owing to the statute of limitations and acquitted the head of the Security Directorate.

The appellate judgments were recorded in a special register on 10 September 2018, the date from which the applicant could obtain a certified copy. They were considered final under domestic law, and the applicant had no right to lodge an appeal in cassation.
001-252386:
The application was lodged by two British nationals, Mr Christopher Stanton and Mr Raymond Bowen, against the United Kingdom. Both were indeterminate sentence prisoners whose release after expiry of their minimum terms depended on a Parole Board risk assessment and, in each case, on residence at designated Approved Premises.

The first applicant was sentenced on 8 October 2010 to an indeterminate sentence of imprisonment for public protection, with a minimum term expiring on 24 May 2013. He was moved to open prison conditions on 4 February 2014. On 13 February 2015 his offender manager contacted Mandeville House Approved Premises, asking for a place as part of his release risk-management plan; she was told a place would become available in July 2015, later confirmed as 23 July 2015. At a Parole Board oral hearing on 26 March 2015, the proposed plan included residence at Mandeville House. On 27 March 2015 the Parole Board directed his release to Mandeville House, noting that a bed was available from 23 July 2015. Further enquiries up to 10 July 2015, including with other Approved Premises in Wales, found no earlier availability. On 6 July 2015 he applied for habeas corpus; it was refused on the papers on 10 July and again after an oral hearing on 21 July 2015, with directions for judicial review. He was released on 23 July 2015, 118 days after the Parole Board decision, and stayed at Mandeville House for almost 11 weeks. He had periods of release on temporary licence on 29 April and 6 July 2015.

The second applicant was convicted of murdering his wife and sentenced on 29 May 1998 to life imprisonment, with a 14-year minimum term expiring on 22 August 2011. He was moved to open prison on 31 October 2012. His offender manager contacted Mandeville House in February 2014 and was told no place would be available until 21 January 2015. His oral hearing was later listed for 30 October 2014. At that hearing the probation service recommended release to Approved Premises because his risk of harm was assessed as high, and the Parole Board was told no guaranteed bed existed before January 2015. On 13 November 2014 the Parole Board directed release subject to licence conditions including residence at Mandeville House. Communications and enquiries with Mandeville House and other Approved Premises in Gloucester, Bristol and Swansea found no earlier space. He issued habeas corpus and judicial review applications on 15 December 2014; the habeas corpus application was ultimately withdrawn on 16 January 2015 after release was confirmed for 21 January. He was released to Mandeville House on 21 January 2015, 69 days after the Parole Board decision, and stayed eight weeks.

In domestic judicial review proceedings, both applicants alleged that continued detention after the Parole Board decisions breached section 28 of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997 and Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention. The High Court dismissed their claims on 5 August 2016, finding the delays reasonable and no systemic insufficiency of Approved Premises. The Court of Appeal refused permission to appeal on the Convention grounds and dismissed the appeals on 20 December 2017, addressing statutory interpretation, reasonableness and the “chain of causation”. The Supreme Court refused permission to appeal on 18 March 2019.
001-252389:
The applicants are three Moldovan nationals, Galina Roşca and others. On 14 March 2015 they lodged an application alleging a breach of the principle of legal certainty and complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

R.P. had four children: R.I., R.T., R.G. and R.Gr. R.P. died in April 2000. By will, he left plots of land (“the testate property”) to R.I. Within six months of R.P.’s death, R.I. formally accepted the succession under the will and on 8 November 2000 received a certificate as heir to the testate property. The first applicant had been married to R.G. until his death before R.P.’s death. The second and third applicants are their children. Before R.P. died, the applicants lived on his property and continued to live there afterwards.

In February 2011 R.I., represented by G.A., obtained from the notary handling R.P.’s succession a certificate attesting his right to part of the property not covered by the will. He donated that property to G.V. On 29 March 2011 G.V. brought court proceedings seeking the applicants’ removal from the disputed property. On 30 March 2011 the applicants counterclaimed, seeking annulment of the certificate recognising R.I. as heir to the intestate part and of the donation to G.V., and recognition that they had de facto accepted R.P.’s succession by living on the property.

On 15 November 2011 the Criuleni District Court accepted G.V.’s claims and rejected the applicants’ claims. It found that R.I. had accepted the succession within six months and that, because R.G. was already dead when R.P. died, the applicants had no right to the property as R.G.’s heirs by law.

On 15 May 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal overturned that judgment and accepted the applicants’ claims. It found that the applicants had taken the rank R.G. would have had if alive when R.P. died. They had de facto accepted the succession by living on the property. It also found that none of R.P.’s other children, including R.I., had accepted the succession of the property not covered by the will within six months. R.I. had missed the six-month deadline and, when he acted in February 2011, had done so through a representative, G.A., contrary to law. The court found that R.I. “did not have the legal or moral right to [the disputed property]”.

R.I. and G.V. appealed on points of law. They argued that R.I.’s acceptance within six months covered the entire property he could inherit, both the testate property and his share of the remainder. They said the Court of Appeal had ignored R.I.’s formal acceptance and that, under the applicable law, accepting a succession covered the whole estate.

On 2 January 2013 the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the lower judgment. It found that in 2000 R.I. had requested only a certificate based on the will, not one for intestate inheritance, which he requested in 2011. On 30 April 2014 the same court rejected an extraordinary appeal by R.Gr., who complained that he had not been involved in the proceedings and that the higher courts had not reacted to notarised declarations by two of R.P.’s nieces and nephews, including applicant Ms Roșca Diana, stating that they refused to inherit R.P.’s property.

On 27 May 2013 the applicants brought a second set of proceedings against the notary, asking to annul the certificate attesting that Roșca Andrei, the second applicant, was heir to one quarter of the intestate part, and to replace it with certificates giving each of the three applicants one third of that property. On 11 December 2013 the Criuleni District Court accepted their claims, finding that facts established in a final court decision did not have to be proved again and could not be contested in later proceedings. On 30 July 2014 the Chișinău Court of Appeal set that decision aside and rejected the claims. It found that the 15 May 2012 judgment, although final, had only established the applicants’ right to inherit, not that they were the only heirs. Since R.I. had also accepted the succession within six months, he had the right to obtain part of the property not covered by the will. The applicants appealed, arguing that the Court of Appeal had not properly considered the 15 May 2012 judgment, which had established that R.I. had no right to the disputed property. On 3 December 2014 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded.
001-252395:
The applications were lodged against the Italian Republic by three applicants. The first, Ornella Orlando, is an Italian national born in 1982, living in Naples, represented by Luca Strazzullo. The second, Giovanna De Vincentiis (listed in the appended table as De Vicentiis), is an Italian national born in 1957, living in Castiglione Messer Raimondo, represented by Vincenzo Luca Salini. The third, Agenzia Ofelia di Delia Mercuri, is a company registered in Italy in 1996, based in Caulonia, represented by Maria Carmela Mirarchi. Their applications were lodged on 25 February 2015 (no. 10868/15), 5 August 2023 (no. 31961/23) and 4 August 2023 (no. 31978/23).

The case as presented concerns the refusal by the domestic administrative courts to grant reimbursement of costs which the applicants had incurred in disputes successfully lodged against the State. On various dates, the applicants had instituted proceedings before the regional administrative courts (Tribunali Amministrativi Regionali – TAR) against different domestic authorities, complaining that their requests for access to documents concerning administrative procedures had been dismissed.

In the first applicant’s case, the TAR dismissed her claim. She appealed to the Consiglio di Stato. On 26 August 2014, the Consiglio di Stato upheld one of her grounds of appeal and granted access to the documents. It held that, in the light of the circumstances, the parties should bear their own costs.

In the second applicant’s case, on 12 June 2022 she notified the authority concerned of her action before the TAR. Subsequently, she was notified that the authority had granted access to the documents. She informed the TAR and requested termination of the proceedings. On 17 October 2022, the TAR terminated the proceedings and held that the parties had to bear their own costs (spese compensate). The second applicant appealed to the Consiglio di Stato, which on 7 April 2023 dismissed her claim, observing that the administrative courts enjoy broad discretion and may consider there to be justified reasons for the parties to bear their own costs.

In the third applicant’s case, the TAR upheld its claim and held that the authority concerned had to reimburse EUR 200 to cover the costs of legal representation incurred by the third applicant and the registration fee (contributo unificato). The third applicant appealed to the Consiglio di Stato, arguing that the amount awarded was insufficient compared with the expenses actually incurred. On 18 April 2023, the Consiglio di Stato dismissed the appeal. It observed that a lump-sum award to cover costs incurred by the successful party was an established practice and that the administrative courts were not required to refer to the minimum scale of fees set out in Decree no. 55 of 10 March 2014 of the Ministry of Justice. In the circumstances of the case and in the light of the simplified nature of the proceedings, the sum was considered reasonable.

The applicants complained of a breach of their right of access to a court, guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, owing to the refusal by the administrative courts to grant reimbursement of the costs incurred in the proceedings. They also raised the same complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention and/or Article 13 of the Convention.
001-252505:
The case *Parun and Others v. Türkiye* comprises applications nos. 9991/20 and 344 others lodged against Türkiye under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants are listed in the appended table and are Turkish nationals resident in various places, some represented by lawyers. The applications were lodged on the various dates indicated in that table, beginning with 6 February 2020 and continuing thereafter. The Turkish Government were represented by Abdullah Aydın, Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice. The Court gave notice of complaints under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 7 (no punishment without law) to the Government, and the parties submitted observations.

The case concerns the applicants’ convictions for membership of an armed terrorist organisation described by the Turkish authorities as the “Fetullahist Terror Organisation/Parallel State Structure” (FETÖ/PDY), which the authorities considered to be behind the coup attempt in Türkiye on 15 July 2016. The broader domestic background and context were set out in the earlier case of *Yüksel Yalçınkaya v. Türkiye* ([GC], no. 15669/20).

The applicants’ convictions were based decisively on their use of an encrypted messaging application named “ByLock”. The domestic authorities and courts considered that ByLock was designed for the exclusive use of FETÖ/PDY members and that establishing use of that application was sufficient on its own for conviction under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code for membership of an armed terrorist organisation.

Other evidence against the applicants, if any, mainly involved: an admission of using ByLock; decrypted message content confirming use of that application; or witness statements attesting to such use. It also included membership of a trade union, association and/or foundation considered affiliated with FETÖ/PDY; account activities at Bank Asya, considered part of the organisation’s financial structure; possession of pro-FETÖ/PDY publications or other audio-visual material; participation in trips considered organised by FETÖ/PDY and records of exit from and entry to Türkiye; donations to FETÖ/PDY-affiliated foundations; participation in demonstrations considered supportive of FETÖ/PDY or in other organisational activities; social media posts in favour of the organisation; residence in FETÖ/PDY student houses or dormitories; use of other messaging applications such as Kakao Talk or Eagle to communicate with other members; Historical Traffic Search (HTS) records indicating communications with others prosecuted for the same offence or other digital evidence suggesting membership; employment by and/or membership of FETÖ/PDY-affiliated institutions, organisations or companies; and witness statements regarding such employment, membership or other connections to FETÖ/PDY.

In some applicants’ cases, convictions were imposed without waiting for the submission to the case files of detailed ByLock findings and evaluation reports—potentially including decrypted content of communications over ByLock—on the ground that establishing use of that application sufficed for conviction, irrespective of the nature and content of the communications.

The applicants lodged individual applications with the Constitutional Court against their convictions. That court summarily dismissed those applications as inadmissible, relying on its case-law endorsing the Court of Cassation’s landmark judgments on the matter, as described in *Yüksel Yalçınkaya*.
001-252514:
The applicant is the Christian Religious Organization of Jehovah’s Witnesses, a religious organisation registered in Armenia. In 2009 it purchased three plots of land in different parts of Yerevan. The ownership certificates issued in its name indicated that all three plots were designated for the construction of public buildings.

On 10 December 2012 the applicant lodged three separate applications with the Yerevan mayor’s office seeking planning permissions, which were a prerequisite for obtaining building permits and constructing religious buildings on the plots. In two letters dated 20 December 2012, the mayor’s office refused two applications. It alleged that there had been incidents in which the construction of religious buildings had led to complaints and intolerance by neighbouring residents, and considered the construction of such buildings in residential areas inappropriate. On 21 December 2012, with respect to the third application, the mayor’s office stated that it was dealing with urban development issues in the area and would address the matter after that process was completed.

On 8 February 2013 the applicant appealed to the mayor, requesting that the replies of 20 and 21 December 2012 be set aside and that planning permissions and building permits be issued for all three plots. In support, it submitted copies of planning permissions granted in 2009 to the previous owners of two plots for the construction of public buildings. Those permissions expressly stated that the plots were located in a mixed-development zone. On 25 February 2013 the mayor’s office replied that it considered the construction of religious buildings in residential areas unacceptable because it would lead to complaints from neighbouring residents.

On 1 April 2013 the applicant lodged a claim with the Administrative Court. It requested that the mayor’s office decisions be set aside, that the alleged inaction of the mayor on its appeal be declared unlawful, and that the mayor’s office be obliged to issue planning permissions. It also alleged a breach of its freedom of religion and of the right not to be discriminated against.

On 31 March 2014 one department of the mayor’s office sent an internal letter to another department, stating that the construction of religious buildings on all three plots was incompatible with the relevant urban zoning plans. According to that letter, one plot was in an industrial zone, another in a recreational zone, and the third was partly in a multi-storey residential development zone and partly in a mixed-development zone.

On 1 December 2014 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s claims. It reasoned that the construction of religious buildings in the community was a matter of social and cultural policy falling within the mayor’s discretion, and that the courts had limited jurisdiction. It further found the applicant’s Convention complaints unfounded because the refusals had not been based on its religious beliefs but on the view that the construction of religious buildings of any denomination was inappropriate in the specific locations. The applicant appealed.

On 27 May 2015 the Administrative Court of Appeal partly upheld the judgment. It considered that the Administrative Court had given an expansive interpretation to the mayor’s discretion, which might incorrectly imply that the mayor’s actions were not subject to judicial review, but found that the outcome had been correctly determined. It considered that, absent evidence that the urban zoning plan permitted the construction of a place of worship, public opinion had to be taken into account. It referred to the internal letter of 31 March 2014 and considered that the request to oblige the mayor’s office to issue planning permissions could not be granted. It discontinued the proceedings in respect of the remaining claims, finding that they were not subject to judicial review. The applicant lodged a further appeal with the Court of Cassation, which was declared inadmissible for lack of merit on 29 July 2015.

The applicant organisation lodged application no. 5142/16 against Armenia with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 January 2016.
001-252518:
Marina Anatolyevna Kovtun, born in 1967, a Russian national, was the applicant. She was represented by A. Shadrin. The Ukrainian Government was represented by M. Sokorenko. The applicant complained under Article 5 § 3 that her detention was unjustified and under Article 6 § 2 that a security service official’s public statement violated her presumption of innocence.

On 16 November 2014 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of joining two Russian clandestine organisations seeking to undermine Ukraine’s territorial integrity. She was alleged to have attended briefings and undergone training in Russia for sabotage, obtained and stored explosive devices and weapons, and orchestrated explosions, including the Stena Bar explosion in Kharkiv in November 2014, which injured 13 people. She was charged with involvement in unlawful attacks on Ukraine’s territorial integrity, commission of a terrorist act with serious consequences, and unlawful possession of firearms and explosives.

In applications for pre-trial detention and later extensions, prosecutors relied on her links with pro-Russia individuals and persons in Russia involved in intelligence and subversive activities against Ukraine. On 18 November 2014 the Kharkiv Kyivskyi District Court remanded her in custody. It found reasonable suspicion based on search results and witness statements, and relied on evidence of links with pro-Russia individuals and Russian nationals suspected of subversive activities and sabotage. It found risks of absconding and reoffending because of those links, the “systematic nature” of activities involving several individuals including persons from Russia, and repeated explosions. The District Court extended detention approximately every two months, citing continued risks and the need for additional investigations. Some decisions referred to the “Bail Exclusion Clause”, which at the relevant time precluded non-custodial preventive measures for defendants accused of terrorism and other national security offences. Appeals upheld the detention orders. On 7 October 2019 the District Court convicted her of involvement in terrorist acts and unlawful possession of firearms and explosives, sentencing her to 11 years’ imprisonment. In December 2019 she was transferred to Russia in a prisoner exchange.

On 18 February 2015 Mr P., head of the Security Service of Ukraine in the Kharkiv Region, held a press briefing. He said the SBU was identifying and arresting members of “terrorist groups, saboteurs and separatists”, some of whom were being sent to Russia in prisoner exchanges. Responding to a question about the Stena Bar bomb, he said that “except for Marina Kovtun, who was the orchestrator of the explosion”, regional prosecutors and he had contacted the Prosecutor General, who supported removing her name from an exchange list. He stated the Prosecutor General’s position was that she “had real blood on her hands”, unlike in respect of other explosions. He added that another co-conspirator in the Stena Bar explosion had been arrested that year for supplying her with weapons, recalled images from a search of her garage showing many weapons, and said the accomplice was under investigation.

The applicant lodged a defamation claim, arguing that the statements implying her involvement in the explosion violated her presumption of innocence. The courts dismissed the claim. The first-instance court stated that the relevant passages concerned her involvement in a possible prisoner exchange rather than commission of a specific offence; that P. had merely reported the Prosecutor General’s position that there were no grounds for her exchange; and that the remarks did not refer to her full name, including her patronymic. On 4 April 2018 the Supreme Court upheld the lower courts’ decisions, stating that the impugned statement was intended to inform the public about criminal offences under investigation at the time.
001-252525:
M.C., a Serbian national born in 1978 who lived in Jászapáti, had resided in Hungary since 2010 for employment purposes. On 22 February 2022 he lodged a request for a residence permit for employment. On 25 April 2022 the National Directorate-General for Aliens Policing (NDGAP) dismissed the application, relying on an opinion from the Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok police department that his residence posed a threat to public safety. He appealed. On 7 July 2022 the NDGAP at second instance quashed the first-instance decision, finding, on the basis of a police opinion obtained in the appeal, that he did not constitute a risk, and remitted the case.

On 13 October 2022, in the resumed proceedings, the NDGAP dismissed the application and expelled him to Serbia. It held that the conditions for a residence permit concerning employment, housing, sufficient means and health insurance were met. However, the Constitution Protection Office (CPO), in an opinion of 27 September 2022, established that he posed a threat to national security. The NDGAP therefore dismissed the request under sections 13(1)(h) and 18(1)(a) of Act no. II of 2007 on the admission and right of residence of third-country nationals. The underlying information in the CPO assessment was classified under Act no. CLV of 2009 on the protection of classified information.

The applicant appealed. In the appeal proceedings, the CPO maintained its findings concerning the national security risk. Relying on that assessment, the NDGAP at second instance emphasised that, given the CPO’s opinion, consideration of any other conditions was excluded.

The applicant sought judicial review. On 5 April 2023 the Debrecen High Court dismissed his action. It held that the NDGAP was not bound by the CPO’s assessment, but, in the absence of any circumstances suggesting otherwise, it based its decision exclusively on that assessment. It explained that there was no opportunity to consider the applicant’s personal circumstances, since the existence of a national security risk made rejection of the residence permit compulsory. Such risk had been established by the CPO. The trial judge consulted the classified documents and confirmed the CPO’s assessment. On 20 June 2023 the Kúria declared the applicant’s petition for judicial review inadmissible. The applicant did not lodge a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court.

Meanwhile, the applicant requested access to the CPO’s classified report under the Classified Information Act. On 11 November 2022 the CPO rejected his application. His request for judicial review of that rejection was to no avail.

In unrelated constitutional complaint cases, the Constitutional Court found that whether an individual’s presence in Hungary constituted a threat to national security could not be reassessed in constitutional proceedings, as that would amount to re-examination of the facts; that task belonged to ordinary courts. It also held that it could not review access to classified information and related procedural questions where those had not been subject to the immigration proceedings concerned by the constitutional complaint.

The applicant complained under Article 8 that, for want of any connection with his country of origin, his expulsion violated his right to respect for his private life. He further complained that he had been expelled without sufficient procedural guarantees. Relying on Article 13, he submitted that, without access to the grounds of the alleged national security risk, he had had no effective remedy against the expulsion decision.
001-252527:
K.A., a Moroccan national born in 1966, lives in Oroklini/Larnaca and is represented by N. Charalambidou, lodged an application against Cyprus on 13 February 2025. The application concerns his detention on national security grounds from 10 January 2019 until 24 February 2020 and the procedural fairness of domestic proceedings nos. 422/2019 and 78/2019, by which he challenged that detention. The Cypriot Government is represented by the Attorney General.

On 10 January 2019, after entering Cyprus irregularly through the occupied areas, K.A. applied for asylum with the Aliens and Immigration Service of the Cyprus Police (AIS). The same day, he was interviewed by the Counter Terrorism Office (CTO) and the Cyprus Intelligence Service (CIS) after being flagged as a “category B suspect” in a foreign service database collaborating with the CTO. The foreign service confirmed that day that he was suspected of involvement in terrorism-related operations in support of a terrorist group. The CTO considered him a threat to public order and national security and informed the relevant authorities.

On that basis, the Deputy Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department (CRMD) ordered his detention on national security grounds under section 9ΣΤ(2)(e) of the Refugee Law, which permits detention of an asylum seeker where protection of national security or public order so requires. He was informed the same day, placed in police custody, and transferred to the Menoyia Detention Centre for Prohibited Immigrants, where he remained throughout his detention.

In asylum proceedings, on 12 April 2019 the Asylum Service recognised K.A. as a refugee but revoked his refugee status under section 6A(1)(c) of the Refugee Law, considering him a threat or danger to State security, and ultimately rejected his application for international protection. He appealed to the Reviewing Authority for Refugees, which upheld the decision on 30 July 2019. On 14 October 2019 he lodged recourse no. 229/19 with the Administrative Court for International Protection; those proceedings remain pending and have suspensive effect.

As to the lawfulness of detention, on 22 March 2019 K.A. asked the Administrative Court to set aside the detention order as unlawful (recourse no. 422/2019). On 22 April 2019 the Administrative Court dismissed the recourse, holding the order lawful. It relied on three confidential documents submitted by the State after K.A. complained that no evidence justifying the national-security assessment had been disclosed: a classified CTO letter to the Attorney General dated 18 April 2019; a memorandum between Cyprus and a foreign State on terrorism-related information exchange; and an implementation guide. At the State’s request, these were not disclosed to K.A. The domestic court considered this did not breach his fair-trial rights because disclosure could be limited where it might hinder investigations, and its own access offset any disadvantage. It found the detention based on an individualised assessment and information indicating suspected terrorism involvement. The decisive factor was that K.A. had been flagged in a cooperating foreign State’s database as a terrorism suspect, which alone justified detention; the court saw no reason to doubt the source and found alternatives insufficient.

On 6 May 2019 K.A. appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 78/2019). On 16 October 2024 the Supreme Constitutional Court unanimously dismissed the appeal, upholding the lower court’s findings.

After inspecting administrative files held by the Asylum Service, K.A. submitted that he saw a letter dated 28 January 2019 from the AIS to the head of the Asylum Service. It allegedly stated he was suspected of operational activity supporting a terrorist group, that his statements were inconsistent about trips and his lost passport later found in his possession, and that partner agencies reported suspicions by Belgian, French and Spanish police of offences including illegal entry, rape, sexual assault, fraud, forgery, false documents, resisting arrest, disobeying authorities, and threatening to bomb the Belgian consulate in Morocco in May 2011. It concluded his presence posed a security risk.

On 17 July 2019 K.A. petitioned the Supreme Court for habeas corpus (no. 126/2019), claiming detention had lasted too long. On 5 August 2019 the Supreme Court dismissed it, noting his refugee status had been revoked and continued detention was linked to pending administrative procedures. On 20 November 2019 the CRMD requested an update from the AIS. On 19 December 2019 the AIS confirmed the risk and threat remained. On 16 January 2020 the CRMD decided to continue detention. On 17 January 2020 K.A. filed a second habeas corpus petition (no. 4/2020), challenging the length of detention.

On 24 February 2020 the Supreme Court ordered his release, holding that the State had failed to justify continued detention and had provided neither the material submitted to the Administrative Court nor substantive evidence from the 16 January 2020 review. The same day, the CRMD revoked the detention order and released him; no deportation order could be issued while recourse no. 229/2019 was pending. He currently resides in Larnaca at an address known to the authorities.
001-252624:
Anar Mammadov, an Azerbaijani national born in 1979 and living in Baku, is a journalist and chief editor of the news website criminal.az. He had been formally warned by prosecuting authorities in 2015 and 2017 over articles alleged to contain false and biased information. On 3 July 2018 an assassination attempt was made on E.V., head of the Ganja City Executive Authority, leaving him and his bodyguard seriously injured. Riots followed in Ganja, during which two police officers were killed. Between 3 and 5 July 2018 the applicant published articles discussing possible causes of the attack. Two articles later formed the basis of charges against him.

On 9 July 2018 the Prosecutor General’s Office stated that certain media had spread false and provocative information about a “premeditated act of terror,” inciting terrorism, forcible seizure of power and constitutional change. Criminal proceedings were instituted under Articles 214-2 and 281.1 of the Criminal Code, and also under Article 313 regarding criminal.az and other websites. The same day the applicant was questioned by the Baku City Prosecutor’s Office for several hours without a lawyer. He claimed investigators seized and examined his two mobile telephones without a court order. He was required to sign a dictated statement consenting to hand over two mobile telephones, two laptops and criminal.az-related documents for the Article 313 investigation. An investigator then issued a seizure decision relying on Article 243.3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The applicants, Dina Schoonbeek and Albert Johan Veldsink, are Dutch nationals born in 1962 and 1968, living in Dedemsvaart. They were represented by lawyer D.G.J. Sanderink. The respondent Government is the Netherlands.

On 2 May 2019 the municipal executive of Hardenberg ordered the applicants, subject to a penalty payment, to remove modular building units from their land because they had been installed in violation of the municipality’s zoning plan. The applicants challenged those decisions. The Overijssel Regional Court dismissed their appeal. The applicants then lodged a further appeal with the Administrative Jurisdiction Division of the Council of State. Besides disagreeing with the Regional Court on the merits, they relied on the Court’s judgment in *Zustović v. Croatia* and requested full reimbursement of their legal expenses if their further appeal was upheld, instead of compensation under the flat-rate system for legal expenses in administrative proceedings. They argued that the flat-rate amount was so low compared with their actual legal expenses that its application would breach their right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1. They submitted that actual expenses in the further appeal had so far amounted to EUR 12,931.83, while expenses in the previous proceedings had amounted to EUR 5,500. Under the flat-rate system, they said, compensation was calculated by points for procedural acts at EUR 748 per point; one point was awarded for lodging an appeal and one for attending a hearing, so compensation was unlikely to exceed EUR 1,496 for the further appeal.

On 9 February 2022 the Administrative Jurisdiction Division upheld the further appeal but did not award full legal expenses. It awarded EUR 3,795 under the flat-rate system for the appeal and further appeal, plus EUR 439 for court fees. The Division recognised that this interfered with the applicants’ right of access to a court, since they had to bear a significant amount of legal expenses. Referring to *Černius and Rinkevičius v. Lithuania*, it stated that such interference could be justified if the essence of the right was not impaired and if it pursued a legitimate aim and was proportionate. It found that the flat-rate system aimed to limit public expenditure, keep costs rules straightforward and relieve administrative courts. It noted similar systems in Germany, Belgium, Austria and France. It considered the interference proportionate because, unlike in *Zustović*, the applicants received some compensation. It found *Zustović* specific to Croatia and not a departure from *Černius and Rinkevičius*. It also noted that the applicants were not at risk of having to pay the other side’s costs, that administrative court fees were generally limited, that flat-rate compensation was generally sufficient for legal-aid users, and that non-legal-aid applicants could be considered to have sufficient resources. Domestic courts had discretion to award higher compensation depending on complexity, interests and procedural acts.

Under domestic law, the General Administrative Law Act permits objection, appeal and further appeal, with court fees. Section 7:15(2) provides for reimbursement in objection procedures where a decision is revoked for unlawfulness. Section 8:75 allows an administrative court to order payment of reasonable costs. The Decree on costs in administrative-law proceedings specifies eligible costs and rates. Compensation is calculated by assigning points to procedural acts, multiplied by a fixed value and an adjustment coefficient for complexity and joined cases. At the time of the Administrative Jurisdiction Division’s judgment, one point in appeal and further appeal was EUR 759, and one point in objection proceedings was EUR 541. Standard rates may be departed from in exceptional circumstances.

The applicant, Mr Hüseyın Baybasın, a Turkish national born in 1956, is serving a life sentence in the Netherlands. At the relevant time he was detained at De Schie Prison in Rotterdam; he is now detained in Lelystad. He was represented by lawyer J. Serrarens. The Netherlands Government were represented by B. Koopman.

On 10 February 2021 the applicant received an unsupervised visit from his lawyer in a meeting room. Afterwards he was required to press a “randomiser” button. The light turned red, and he was subjected to a strip search (visitatie).

On 16 February 2021 he complained to the Complaints Commission of De Schie’s Supervisory Board. He alleged that the strip search after a privileged lawyer visit breached Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. He argued there was no reason for it: he had never been found with prohibited items during nearly 25 years’ imprisonment, and his lawyers’ conduct had always been beyond reproach.

On 16 March 2021 the chairperson declared the complaint manifestly ill-founded. The chairperson accepted that the applicant found the search uncomfortable and degrading, especially given no prior prohibited items, but considered that prison vigilance made it not unreasonable or unfair to require prisoners to press the randomiser after meeting an external visitor, including a privileged visitor.

On 24 March 2021 the applicant appealed. He repeated his arguments: prison vigilance did not justify such an intrusive infringement of physical integrity; there was no specific reason to suspect his lawyer had given him prohibited items. He said that in his experience the randomiser turned red considerably more than half the time. He also noted there was no precedent at De Schie for lawyers smuggling prohibited items, and the governor had not mentioned any such incidents before the Complaints Commission.

On 5 November 2021 the deputy governor responded, citing domestic RSJ case-law. He submitted that strip searches after privileged visits were permitted and could be based on a randomiser, which was unpredictable and could not be influenced. The absence of prior finds did not reduce the risk on this occasion; it showed the system worked. On 8 December 2021 the applicant replied that the randomiser could be set manually; staff had occasionally set it green when there was no time for strip searches, and he had heard it could also be set red. On 25 January 2022 the appellate judge of the RSJ Appeals Board declared the appeal ill-founded. No further appeal lay.

Domestically, section 29 of the Prisons Act authorises a governor to search a prisoner’s person or clothing on arrival or departure, before or after a visit, or when necessary for order or security. A personal search includes external visual observation of bodily orifices, in a private room and, where possible, by same-sex staff. The Explanatory Memorandum allows searches at random or on specific suspicions. De Schie house rules and instructions provided that after visits prisoners pressed a randomiser: green meant frisk, red meant strip search. They stated strip searches after social or official visits were possible only if there were reasons/serious suspicions or if ordered, while also describing random selection. Complaints went to the Complaints Commission, with appeal to an RSJ Appeals Board. RSJ case-law treated random strip searches after visits, including lawyer visits, as permissible if not more than twice a month on average.

On 3 February 2017 Daci applied through the Ombudsperson for a position on the vetting bodies. On 13 February 2017 the Ombudsperson’s ad hoc commission and the International Monitoring Operation adopted a protocol under which a self-declaration was sufficient to presume compliance with section 6(1)(dh) of the Vetting Act. At a parliamentary hearing on 2 June 2017, Daci said he had been a judge from 1993 to 1997. When asked whether he had left voluntarily or been removed, he said he had resigned. Parliament appointed him a Special Appeal Chamber judge on 17 June 2017.

In 2020, following a criminal complaint by B.C., the Special Prosecution Office against Corruption and Organised Crime investigated Daci for falsifying a “form” under Article 190 of the Criminal Code; the charge was reclassified as falsifying a document under Article 186. It held that the application was a formal act required by section 7 of the Vetting Act and constituted a document under Article 186; it relied on earlier case-law on intellectual falsification, found that Daci had benefited by being appointed and had misled the parliamentary committee. Atresmedia Corporación de Medios de Comunicación S.A., a private Spanish broadcasting group based in San Sebastián de los Reyes, operates channels including Antena 3 and La Sexta. Ahead of national parliamentary elections on 28 April 2019, it planned a televised debate for 23 April 2019 between five candidates for Prime Minister, representing PP, PSOE, Unidas Podemos, Ciudadanos and Vox. It selected these parties as nationally present forces expected, according to a March 2019 CIS survey, to obtain over 10% of the vote. Four of them, all except Vox, had won seats in the June 2016 general elections; Vox had received 0.2% then, but obtained 10.96% in the December 2018 Andalusian elections, and the CIS survey estimated 11.9% for Vox.

Three regional parties—Coalición Canaria, Junts and EAJ-PNV—complained to the Central Electoral Commission (CEC). They argued that the planned debate breached section 66(2) of the LOREG and the principles of pluralism, proportionality, equality and neutrality, because Vox was included although it had not secured representation in the previous equivalent elections and was not a significant political group. They asked the CEC to require Atresmedia to cancel the debate without them or give them compensatory airtime. Atresmedia replied that Vox was a relevant national contender, with nationwide lists and strong polling, and offered airtime and other programmes to the complainants.

By decision of 16 April 2019, the CEC upheld the complaints. Referring to section 66(2) LOREG and Instruction no. 4/2011, it held that private television broadcasters had to apply proportionality by reference to results in the most recent equivalent elections; Vox did not qualify as a significant political group at national level because it lacked 5% of valid votes. The CEC concluded that the five-candidate debate could not be held as proposed and had to be modified to comply with proportionality.

Atresmedia appealed to the Supreme Court on 12 June 2019, later formalising its claims on 11 September 2019. It sought annulment of the CEC decision and a declaration that section 8(2) of Instruction no. 4/2011 was null. It argued that the restriction breached Article 20 of the Spanish Constitution and Articles 53 and 81; that the Instruction exceeded the CEC’s remit and imposed a single debate format; and that the measure lacked a legitimate aim and was disproportionate, favouring established parties and depriving voters of information. Vox withdrew from the proceedings. On 25 February 2021 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding no breach of the Constitution or domestic law. It held that the relevant principles derived from the LOREG, that the Instruction did not impose a single format, and that compensatory airtime or debates were possible.

On 5 April 2021 Atresmedia lodged an amparo appeal, relying on Article 20 § 1 in conjunction with Articles 23, 53 § 1 and 81 § 1 of the Constitution. On 27 March 2023 the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible, finding no clear violation of a fundamental right protectable in amparo.

After the CEC decision, Atresmedia held the debate on 23 April 2019 without Vox, with four candidates, broadcast on Antena 3, La Sexta, Onda Cero and Atresplayer. TVE held a separate debate on 22 April 2019 with the same four parties. Vox received 10.26% in the 28 April 2019 elections and won parliamentary representation. After new elections were called for 10 November 2019, Atresmedia broadcast a La Sexta debate with eight parties, including Vox. Atresmedia lodged its application with the European Court of Human Rights on 26 July 2023.

The case concerns applications lodged against Türkiye by Turkish nationals listed in the appended table on various dates. The applicants alleged under Article 5, among other things, a lack of reasonable suspicion that they had committed an offence, a lack of relevant and sufficient reasons for ordering and extending their pre-trial detention, the length of that detention, and the ineffectiveness of judicial review of the lawfulness of detention.

The factual background is the aftermath of the attempted coup d’état of 15 July 2016. A state of emergency was declared between 21 July 2016 and 18 July 2018, and a notice of derogation was given to the Secretary General of the Council of Europe. The Turkish authorities considered an organisation described as the “Fetullahist Terror Organisation/Parallel State Structure” (FETÖ/PDY) to be behind the attempted coup.

On various dates, the applicants were arrested and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of membership of FETÖ/PDY, an offence punishable under Article 314 of the Criminal Code. Challenges brought by them against their detention were dismissed at the domestic level. During the ensuing criminal investigations and trials, the competent judicial authorities ordered the applicants’ continued detention on various dates. The applicants were held in custody for periods of up to 11 months and 10 days.

When ordering and extending the applicants’ pre-trial detention, the competent judicial authorities relied on various evidential grounds. These included, but were not limited to: witness statements alleging that the applicants had taken an active part in the hierarchical structure of FETÖ/PDY; possession of pro-FETÖ/PDY publications; working in, or being a member of, institutions with ties to the organisation or institutions shut down by state-of-emergency legislative decrees; provision of financial support to FETÖ/PDY or linked institutions; attending or holding meetings (sohbet); communication with senior members of the organisation; ensuring communication among FETÖ/PDY members; use of the ByLock encrypted messaging application; staying in FETÖ/PDY houses; and carrying out other activities on the orders of the organisation.

Under Articles 100 and 101 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the competent judicial authorities mainly justified detention not only on the existence of reasonable suspicion but also on the nature and severity of the alleged offence of membership of an illegal armed organisation and because that offence was among the “catalogue” offences listed in Article 100 § 3 of the Code. Without making an individualised assessment, they also relied on the state of the evidence and the risk of the applicants’ absconding and tampering with evidence, and considered that detention was proportionate. In later stages of the proceedings, the judges took into account the time the applicants had spent in pre-trial detention when deciding to extend detention, without explaining the relevance of that factor.

The applicants’ detention was periodically reviewed by the competent courts, either on requests for release or during regular monthly reviews under Article 108 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In subsequent decisions extending detention, the domestic courts largely reiterated the reasoning in the initial detention order. They considered that alternative measures would not be sufficient to ensure the proper conduct of the proceedings.

The applicants lodged one or more individual applications with the Constitutional Court concerning the detention orders. They complained, inter alia, of an alleged lack of reasonable suspicion that they had committed an offence and an alleged lack of reasons justifying the decisions ordering and extending their pre-trial detention.

According to the latest information provided by the parties, most of the applicants were convicted by first-instance courts of membership of an illegal armed organisation, based on evidence that was present at the time of their detention or that appeared later in the proceedings. Some of the criminal proceedings were still pending before the appellate courts or the Constitutional Court.

Devekom DOO Niš, a company registered in Niš, Serbia, lodged an application against Serbia on 31 March 2022. It complains that customs duties it had paid were refunded only after a considerable period and without interest, placing an excessive burden on its possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 2006 the applicant imported goods from Bosnia and Herzegovina and from Croatia under a preferential customs regime, without paying customs duties, relying on domestic legislation and international agreements then in force. The Niš Customs Office issued import declarations between 2 March and 26 October 2006.

In 2009 the first-instance customs authority began a post-clearance check of those declarations. It found that preferential treatment should not have been applied because the imports did not meet the required conditions for preferential origin. In twelve sets of proceedings, it ordered the applicant to pay customs duties, issuing decisions on 30 October, 5 November, 10 November and 11 November 2009. The applicant appealed, but the appeal did not have suspensive effect, so it paid RSD 7,381,148 (approximately EUR 78,360 at the time).

After several remittals, on 13 November 2018 the first-instance customs authority decided, in twelve decisions, that the imported goods were not subject to customs duties. It ordered refund of the amount paid but dismissed the applicant’s claim for interest. The applicant appealed against the refusal of interest. Between 6 June and 16 July 2019 the second-instance customs authority, within the Ministry of Finance, upheld the decisions.

The second-instance authority reasoned that under Article 278 § 1 of the Customs Act in force from 3 May 2010 to 17 June 2019, repayment of a customs debt did not give rise to interest, except under Article 278 § 2 where a decision granting refund was not implemented within three months. It considered that the interest issue was not a customs procedure and that Article 237 of the former Customs Act did not apply. It said the applicant could submit a separate request for interest only if the refund decision was not implemented within three months.

Between 29 July and 29 August 2019 the exact amount paid, RSD 7,381,148 (approximately EUR 62,671 at the time), was refunded to the applicant.

The applicant brought actions before the Administrative Court against the customs authorities’ decisions. The Administrative Court – Niš Division dismissed the claims and upheld the contested decisions in judgments issued between 8 April and 25 October 2021.

The applicant then lodged constitutional appeals concerning the excessive duration and outcome of the customs proceedings and the Administrative Court proceedings. By decisions of 14 October 2021 and 24 February 2022, the Constitutional Court found that the length of the customs proceedings had been excessive and awarded EUR 3,600 in total for non-pecuniary damage. It dismissed the applicant’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning non-payment of interest, stating that the applicant had failed to invoke constitutionally related grounds under Article 58 of the Constitution and that the criteria for opening proceedings were not met. It also held that the contested judgments contained sufficient reasoning and that proper conclusions had been drawn from the established facts.

The record states that inflation in Serbia from 2009 to 2019 amounted to 69.6%. The Government also referred to domestic civil case-law: a Commercial Court in Belgrade judgment of 12 March 2019 awarded interest on overpaid customs from payment to reimbursement, upheld by the Supreme Court of Cassation on 3 February 2022; and a Commercial Court in Niš judgment of 29 October 2020 awarded reimbursement with default interest from the date the claim was filed, upheld by the Commercial Court of Appeal on 26 April 2023.

The application was lodged against Albania by ten Albanian nationals, represented by E. Syziu, a lawyer in Tirana. The Government was represented by O. Moçka, General State Advocate. The applicants complained of an alleged violation of their right of access to the Supreme Court.

On 2 September 1995, the Commission for the Restitution and Compensation of Property recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a 5,878 sq. m plot in Tirana. It restored part of the plot measuring 2,999.6 sq. m, awarded compensation for 2,501.4 sq. m, and granted a right of first refusal over 615 sq. m. The decision’s reasoning stated that the property had an actual surface area of 7,600 sq. m. In 1996, title to the restored property was entered in the land register.

On 12 September 2007, the Immovable Property Registration Office of Tirana informed the applicants that an inconsistency between the restored plot and the accompanying map prevented it from taking further action. On 12 March 2008, the applicants asked the Agency for the Restitution and Compensation of Property, successor to the Commission, to correct the inconsistency. On 18 March 2008, the Agency told them to apply to its regional office under Article 120 of the Code of Administrative Procedure. They did so on 4 April 2008. On 14 November 2008, the regional office dismissed the request for lack of jurisdiction, stating that under section 18 of the Property Act the power to amend the 1995 decision rested with the Agency. On 25 November 2008, the applicants applied to the Agency’s central office. Those proceedings lasted more than three years and were suspended pending Constitutional Court decisions of 2010 and 2011.

On 7 November 2011, the Agency held that the Commission’s decisions were no longer subject to administrative review because it lacked jurisdiction, as they were considered quasi-judicial. It also stated that the 2008 regional-office decision had been lawful, since the central office had then had power to review former commission decisions, but that this jurisdiction had been removed after a 2010 Constitutional Court ruling.

The applicants then brought a civil action in the Tirana District Court, seeking to quash the Agency’s decision and rectify the 1995 Commission decision. On 3 December 2012, the District Court partly allowed the claim. Relying on an expert report, it found that the documents establishing the ancestor’s property rights referred to an outdated unit of measurement. It ordered rectification of the 1995 decision by adding the word “old” to the unit of measurement in the operative part.

The Agency and the State Advocate’s office appealed, arguing inter alia that the claim was time-barred. On 26 June 2014, the Tirana Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment. The correction was entered in the land register.

On 6 April 2022, the Supreme Court reversed the lower courts’ judgment in camera and dismissed the applicants’ claim as time-barred. It held that the applicants should have brought proceedings within 30 days of becoming aware of the discrepancy between the 1995 decision and the accompanying map. Even assuming they had not been aware in 1995, the 30-day time-limit began when the IPRO informed them of the inconsistency. It further found that, rather than lodging an administrative complaint, they should have brought the matter directly before the domestic courts. On 12 October 2022, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional complaint as being of a fourth-instance nature.

Article 120 of the Code of Administrative Procedure allows correction of clerical errors or manifest inaccuracies without altering substance and sets no statutory time-limit. Section 18 of the 2004 Property Act, as amended by law no. 9684/2007, provided that appeals against decisions of former local commissions could be lodged with the Agency’s central office by the expropriated party or the State Advocate’s office, and the expropriated party could then appeal to the Tirana District Court within 30 days of notification.

It found that F.K. could not have used humiliating expressions related to G.G.’s sexual orientation, since that would also have insulted her brother’s memory, and that she had merely asked him to leave.
