001-252930:
The applicants are five Greek nationals whose properties in Amaliada were expropriated. On 31 August 2018 they lodged an application against the Hellenic Republic. The application concerned compensation payable after the expropriation of their properties.

By a joint ministerial decision issued on 11 February 2008 and published in the Official Government Gazette on 25 February 2008, the expropriation of the applicants’ properties was ordered for the construction of a highway. On 24 February 2009 the Greek State applied for determination of the provisional compensation payable. Hearings took place on 15, 29 and 30 October 2009.

By judgment no. 53/2010 of 26 April 2010, the Amaliada Court of First Instance fixed provisional unitary compensation amounts. For the first applicant, it awarded EUR 10.08 per sq. m for plot no. 201 and EUR 5.42 per sq. m for plot no. 206. For the second applicant, it awarded EUR 4.74 per sq. m for plot no. 300 and EUR 4.50 per sq. m for plot no. 305. For the third applicant, it awarded EUR 101.08 per sq. m for plot no. 078. For the fourth applicant, it awarded EUR 101.08 per sq. m for plot no. 079. For the fifth applicant, it awarded EUR 4.74 per sq. m for plots nos. 316 and 318, and EUR 4.28 per sq. m for plot no. 321. The calculation used property values at the dates of the first-instance hearings. The court also held that the non-expropriated parts of the properties would derive a special benefit from the works because they would have access to the highway.

On 20 October 2010 the Greek State applied for determination of the final compensation. After adjournments on 12 May 2011 and 21 March 2013, the hearing took place on 15 January 2015.

The applicants took several steps concerning the alleged benefit to their remaining properties. On 19 January 2011 the first applicant lodged a counterclaim seeking determination of final compensation and challenging the presumption of benefit, and submitted a written request to intervene. At the hearing of 15 January 2015, the first, second and fifth applicants orally requested leave to intervene and challenged the presumption of benefit. The third and fourth applicants challenged the presumption by written submissions filed at that hearing. Separately, on 14 October 2010 the fifth applicant lodged an application seeking determination of final compensation and challenging the presumption of benefit.

By judgment no. 78/2016 of 31 May 2016, the Patras Court of Appeal dismissed as inadmissible the applicants’ claims regarding the presumption of benefit. It held that the first applicant had not complied with Article 33 § 7 of Law no. 2971/2001, which required a challenge within six months of the provisional compensation determination of 26 April 2010. It further held that the oral intervention requests by the first, second and fifth applicants and the written submissions of the third and fourth applicants sought to extend the scope of the final compensation application contrary to national procedural rules. It also found that the fifth applicant’s claims lacked factual details about the affected parts of his properties.

The Patras Court of Appeal then fixed final unitary compensation amounts: EUR 8 per sq. m for plot no. 201 and EUR 2.60 for plot no. 206 (first applicant); EUR 2 per sq. m for plots nos. 300 and 305 (second applicant); EUR 6.50 for plot no. 078 (third applicant); EUR 6.50 for plot no. 079 (fourth applicant); and EUR 2.50 for plots nos. 316, 318 and 350 and EUR 2 for plot no. 321 (fifth applicant). It relied on Article 17 § 2 (c) of the Greek Constitution and Article 13 § 1 (b) of Law no. 2882/2001, under which final compensation is calculated by reference to values at the date of the appellate hearing where more than one year has passed since the provisional-compensation hearing. It also referred to property-value depreciation from 2009 onward. As to plots nos. 078 and 079, they had been recorded within settlement boundaries, an error later rectified, aligning their unit prices with the other plots.

The applicants appealed on points of law, arguing that the appellate court should have used the provisional-compensation hearing date, not the date of its own hearing, as the critical date for final compensation, which resulted in lower awards. They also argued that the appellate court had wrongly dismissed their claims about the presumption of benefit.

By judgment no. 2062/2017, final on 1 March 2018, the Court of Cassation examined the arguments on the merits and dismissed them. It ruled that the relevant constitutional and statutory provisions applied regardless of increases or decreases in property values between the two hearings. It upheld the appellate findings on the presumption of benefit and also held that, in any event, all applicants’ claims lacked sufficient factual details as to the parts of their properties allegedly not benefiting from the works.

The applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, reiterating the arguments made before the domestic courts.
001-252935:
The applicant, Gela Tchigladze, a Georgian national born in 1964 living in Tbilisi, lodged application no. 8684/20 against Georgia. He complained under Article 3 that he had been ill-treated during his arrest and that the related criminal investigation was ineffective, and under Article 6 that the domestic courts had failed to give sufficient reasons for his conviction.

On 21 June 2019, during the dispersal of a demonstration, the applicant was arrested. The arrest occurred more than six hours after police began dispersing demonstrators, when most had left and only a small number remained; some individuals engaged in vandalism and threw objects at police. The administrative arrest report, signed by the applicant, stated that he was arrested for verbally insulting police officers and throwing stones. It noted a scratch on the right side of his waist, a bruise on his left side, and scabs on both shins. The administrative-offence report, also signed by him, referred to Article 166 (disorderly conduct) and Article 173 (disobeying lawful orders or insulting law-enforcement personnel) of the Code of Administrative Offences.

Before the first-instance court, the applicant said he had been talking on the phone in the courtyard of a residential building when demonstrators ran in trying to escape police and he followed them. He “partly agreed” with the charges and said he had been unable to control himself because of the day’s developments; he clarified that he had joined in chanting but claimed a man of his age would not have sworn at police or thrown stones. The arresting officers submitted that he had been aggressive, throwing items and swearing, and that they had chased him and two co-accused to the roof of a building, where he was arrested.

On 21 June 2019 the trial court found the applicant and his co-accused guilty of the administrative offences and fined him GEL 1,500 (approximately EUR 480). It reasoned that he had partly admitted the charges and that the submissions and evidence indicated commission of the offences. The applicant later obtained two medical reports indicating bruises on his chest, a haematoma on his right thigh, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

On 1 July 2019 the applicant appealed, alleging an Article 6 breach because the trial court had failed to distinguish the facts relating specifically to him from those relating to his co-accused. He said he had arrived around midnight to look for his son and stayed to help injured demonstrators; he had been arrested in the courtyard of a residential building and beaten with truncheons before being put in a police car. On 6 August 2019 the appellate court held an oral hearing. It found the lower court’s reasoning not deficient, noting the time and location of the offence and the consistency of the arresting officers’ statements with other evidence. It upheld the conviction but reduced the fine to GEL 1,000 (approximately EUR 320), and informed the prosecuting authorities of the ill-treatment allegations.

On 21 August 2019 a prosecutor questioned the applicant as part of a broader investigation into the dispersal events. He reiterated that he had been ill-treated but said the arrest had occurred on the roof of a residential building; when reminded of his earlier statements, he said he had not paid attention at the time. On 22 August 2019 the prosecutor collected his medical documents and ordered a forensic medical examination. The report, dated 11 March 2021, noted that the injuries were minor and had not caused deterioration of his health. The applicant was granted victim status.

On 27 September 2019 an investigative experiment was conducted with the applicant. Authorities attempted to obtain recordings from surveillance cameras of three private entities, but none could be retrieved because of technical issues or deletion; reports noted that recordings had previously been retrieved in June and July 2019 during the investigation into the dispersal. Co-accused questioned in April and June 2021 said they had not been arrested with the applicant and had seen no signs of ill-treatment or complaints when meeting him. Arresting officers questioned in June 2021; one said he had seen injuries on the applicant, which the applicant then explained had occurred before his arrest.

In 2025 criminal proceedings were instituted in absentia against the then Minister of Internal Affairs. He was charged with organising intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm against more than two persons under Article 117 § 3 of the Criminal Code, for allegedly instructing special forces to use kinetic impact projectiles, tear gas, and water cannon simultaneously without prior warning. Those proceedings are pending, and the broader criminal investigation into the events of 20–21 June 2019 is ongoing.
001-252957:
The application was lodged on 15 July 2013 by five Ukrainian nationals, represented by Kyiv lawyers. The third applicant’s identity was not to be disclosed. The case concerns the dispersal of a demonstration organised by the applicants and resulting issues.

On 2 October 2012 Parliament approved at first reading legislation prohibiting “propaganda of homosexuality”. The applicants notified the Kyiv State Administration of a planned demonstration on Maidan Nezalezhnosti on 8 December 2012 to mark International Human Rights Day and oppose the legislation. On 7 December 2012 the Kyiv District Administrative Court prohibited holding it there. On 28 March 2013 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal rejected an appeal; on 7 November 2013 the Higher Administrative Court rejected the first applicant’s cassation appeal. Also on 7 December 2012 the first applicant informed the administration that the demonstration would be held at a different location on 8 December from 1 to 3 p.m.

At 1 p.m. on 8 December 2012 the applicants arrived and found police already present. They began the demonstration. According to the applicants, police formed a circle preventing the public from seeing or joining. Around 2.10 p.m. two people forced through the police circle, sprayed tear gas and attacked demonstrators. One moved toward the third applicant, swinging her hands; he backed away shielding himself, and the attacker grabbed and pulled his hand. Police then apprehended the second, third, fourth and fifth applicants and took them to a police station under Article 260 of the Code on Administrative Offences. At the station, after checking identity papers, police discovered that the third applicant, who looked and identified as male, was female according to his identity papers. The applicants alleged that police mocked and insulted the third applicant and mockingly asked the others about their sexual orientation. They were released after about three hours.

Domestic administrative offence proceedings followed. On 10 December 2012 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court found the second and fifth applicants guilty under Article 173 (petty hooliganism) for pushing citizens in a crowd; the Kyiv Court of Appeal quashed both decisions on 17 and 21 January 2013 for lack of corpus delicti. Another decision of 10 December 2012 fined the fifth applicant UAH 136 under Article 185 for disobeying a lawful order; that was quashed on 16 January 2013. On 13 December 2012 the first applicant was found guilty under Article 185-1 § 2 for infringing public-event procedure and fined UAH 850; this was upheld on 18 January 2013 and became final. On 17 December 2012 proceedings against the fourth applicant under Article 173 were closed; the court found that G. tried to attack the third applicant and the fourth applicant interposed himself, the incident lasting about fifteen seconds. On 18 December 2012 the third applicant was found guilty under Article 173 for pushing citizens and disrupting public order, but was exempted from liability because the violation was minor; this was upheld on 1 February 2013 and became final.

On 13 June 2013 the second, fourth and fifth applicants brought administrative proceedings challenging their police detention and the disruption of their demonstration. They sought a declaration that the detention was unlawful and non-pecuniary compensation, alleging frustration, psychological distress, helplessness, lost trust in law enforcement, and fear of attending public events. They also alleged police mockery over the LGBTI event and sexual orientation. On 18 September 2013 the fifth applicant’s complaint was not examined due to repeated non-appearance, and that decision became final. On 25 November 2013 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal found the second applicant’s detention unlawful but refused compensation for lack of evidence; the Higher Administrative Court upheld that on 15 January 2014. On 30 July 2014 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court found the fourth applicant’s arrest and detention unlawful but refused compensation for lack of evidence; his appeal was dismissed by the Higher Administrative Court on 9 April 2015. On 16 March 2018 the third applicant’s legal gender, name and surname were changed on his birth certificate to reflect his male gender.

The applicant, Anatoliy Viktorovych Zhytnikov, a Ukrainian national born in 1979 and living in Mykolayiv, worked as a logistics manager at private company R. His duties included submitting documents to customs authorities for the company’s imports. On 15 June 2017 he submitted an electronic customs declaration for goods imported by R., including 45 kg of garlic oil valued at UAH 43,065.73 (about EUR 1,460 at the time). The declaration was accompanied by an electronic copy of a CMR consignment note bearing stamps indicating that sanitary and epidemiological controls had been carried out. Customs cleared the goods and released them into free circulation.

Following information from the Security Service of Ukraine in criminal proceedings concerning alleged offences connected with R.’s activities, the customs authorities obtained letters from sanitary and laboratory authorities. Those authorities stated that no sanitary or epidemiological controls had been carried out for the goods and that R. had made no relevant request. Criminal proceedings concerning the alleged use of forged documents during customs clearance were joined to those proceedings; they were later discontinued without the applicant being notified of any suspicion.

On 1 November 2017 the Mykolayiv customs office drew up a report on a violation of customs rules under Article 483 § 1 of the Customs Code. It alleged that the applicant had submitted a forged CMR document bearing forged stamps confirming sanitary and epidemiological controls and had used it as the basis for moving the goods across the customs border.

On 16 November 2017 the Central District Court of Mykolayiv found the applicant guilty of a customs offence under Article 483 § 1. It held that, as the authorised customs declarant of R., he had submitted a CMR consignment note bearing stamps allegedly confirming sanitary and epidemiological controls, although the competent authorities had stated that no such controls had been carried out. The court imposed a fine of UAH 43,065.73, equal to the value of the goods, and ordered confiscation of the goods. Since the goods had already been released into free circulation and were unavailable for confiscation, the court relied on Article 541 § 2 of the Customs Code, which allowed the value of goods to be recovered by court decision where confiscation from customs violators was impossible. It therefore ordered recovery from the applicant of the value of the goods, also UAH 43,065.73.

On 28 February 2018 the Mykolayiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance decision. It rejected the applicant’s arguments that the alleged forgery of the CMR note and stamps had not been established by expert examination and that he could not be held liable for alleged omissions or wrongdoing of others. Relying on information from the sanitary and laboratory authorities, the Court of Appeal held that the CMR note submitted by the applicant bore forged stamps certifying sanitary and epidemiological controls. It further held that the applicant, as the person authorised to deal with customs matters for R., could be treated as an official of that company for customs liability. It found that the sanction had been imposed within the limits of Article 483 § 1. That decision was final.

On 4 April 2018 two enforcement proceedings were opened: one concerning recovery of the value of the goods and the other concerning recovery of the fine. On 8 April 2025 the State Bailiffs Service received full payment of both amounts—UAH 43,065.73 for the goods’ value (about EUR 950 at the time) and UAH 43,065.73 for the fine—together with enforcement fees and costs. On 14 May 2025 both enforcement proceedings were terminated because the decision had been fully enforced.

The applicant lodged application no. 39259/18 with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 July 2018, complaining under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the sanction imposed in the customs proceedings was unlawful and disproportionate.
001-253155:
The applicant is the Public Association Centre for Information Genderdoc-M, an association registered in Chișinău. The respondent is the Republic of Moldova. The application was lodged on 5 May 2015. The subject matter is the alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation and to punish persons involved in interrupting a gay pride march.

On 17 May 2014 the applicant association organised a march called “A year without discrimination” in Chișinău to mark the international day against homophobia. The march was heavily protected by police and special units, which separated participants from several dozen rather aggressive persons wishing to disrupt it. Some of those persons chanted homophobic slogans and insults and threatened participants with violence, including hanging. C., an Orthodox priest who had repeatedly protested against events organised by the LGBT community, managed to approach the marchers. He wrestled away from D., an organiser who worked for the applicant association, a rainbow flag, tearing it apart. According to D.’s statement to the police, she had been holding the flag firmly and C. hit her hands several times to obtain it. Witnesses E. and M., who also worked for the applicant association, told the police that they had seen C. aggressively wrestle away the flag. In doing so, he hit E. on the shoulder and also hit other participants, who were frightened. The applicant association and witnesses noted that the media followed the march closely and recorded the events. One video apparently showed a priest being stopped by police from reaching demonstrators, resisting them, and breaking free using energetic movements.

Another protestor, G., grabbed a banner from the organisers leading the march and refused to return it or to move, thus blocking their passage. Eventually, participants abandoned the banner and continued the march, while police arrested G.

On 26 June 2014 the applicant association lodged two criminal complaints about the actions of C. and G., notably under Article 184 of the Criminal Code, concerning violation of the right to freedom of assembly by unlawfully impeding a public event, including by applying violence not threatening life or health, and Article 187, concerning robbery. It referred to attempts to block the march and to the fact that the two suspects had openly and forcibly taken two objects from the applicant association’s staff, which were never returned.

On 9 July 2014 a criminal investigation was initiated into the applicant association’s allegations. On 27 October 2014 the responsible prosecutor discontinued the investigation, finding that the suspects’ actions did not amount to a criminal offence but rather an administrative one. He found in particular that it had not been established that the two suspects had acted together. Moreover, in the absence of a forensic report, there was no medical evidence of bodily harm to any march participant. He also found that the three-month prescription applicable to administrative offences prevented pursuing the accused for the administrative offence. That decision was upheld by a higher prosecutor.

On 27 January 2015 the investigating judge of the Chișinău District Court (Râșcani District) annulled the prosecutors’ decisions, finding that not all actions had been taken, notably to verify whether the two suspects had planned and acted together.

On 8 April 2015 the applicant association asked the prosecutor to inform it of the progress of the investigation and whether any decision had been taken. It subsequently found out that the investigation had been reopened and more witnesses heard on 11 February and 9 March 2015, after which the investigation had once more been discontinued on 20 March 2015. The applicant association did not challenge that decision.
001-253158:
The applicant, Oliver Fišić, a Croatian national born in 1968 and living in Brašina, complained that he had been denied access to a tribunal concerning a mayoral decision in a public tender in which he had participated as a bidder. He was represented by B. Radan; the Government by Š. Stažnik.

On 15 March 2017 the mayor of Župa dubrovačka ordered a committee to organise a tender for the lease of public areas for vending stands. The tender, published on 20 March 2017, set eligibility criteria, lease duration, minimum bid amounts and the submission deadline; the best bidder would be selected under the municipality’s Decision. The applicant bid 16 HRK per square metre per day for a vending stand in Brašina; another bidder, N.P., bid 11 HRK for the same location. On 5 April 2017 the committee found both bids timely and compliant. Because the bids differed, it decided under section 13 of the municipality’s Decision that N.P., the previous lessee, be offered the lease at the higher price submitted by the applicant. On 21 April N.P. agreed to pay that higher price. On 26 April 2017 the mayor accepted N.P.’s bid and concluded a lease with her. The applicant objected that the mayoral decision was unlawful. On 27 July 2017 the Municipal Council dismissed the objection, emphasising that section 13 gave priority to previous lessees to ensure legal certainty. On 28 July 2017 the municipality, represented by the mayor, concluded a lease with N.P.

The applicant brought an administrative action in the Split Administrative Court challenging the 26 April 2017 mayoral decision. He argued that misapplication of section 13 disadvantaged him vis-à-vis a lower bidder; that priority should apply only if two identical bids were submitted; and that section 13 did not allow the previous lessee to disclose or match the highest bid. On 9 April 2019 the Split Administrative Court set aside the Municipal Council’s decision of 27 July 2017 but upheld the mayoral decision of 26 April 2017. It noted that, under a practice direction of 28 April 2008, acts granting leases of public areas were administrative acts subject to administrative judicial review; no appeal lay against individual mayoral acts; the Municipal Council therefore lacked competence. It reviewed the mayoral decision and found the facts properly established and the law properly applied. The applicant appealed, repeating his arguments and adding that, had section 13 allowed the previous lessee to disclose or match the highest bid, he would never have submitted a bid. On 24 September 2020 the High Administrative Court quashed the Split judgment and declared the administrative action inadmissible. It held, pursuant to its decision of 26 January 2015 in a specific tender procedure, that decisions on leases of public areas were not administrative acts but acts of property management outside administrative judicial review.

On 1 April 2021 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging violations of fair trial, equality before the law, and entrepreneurial and market freedom, relying on the State’s obligation to ensure equal status of entrepreneurs. On 22 December 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It found the restriction on access to a court constitutionally acceptable given the sufficient and relevant reasons provided by the High Administrative Court. That decision was served on 10 January 2022.

Domestically, section 13 of the municipality’s Decision set a priority order for previous lessees, war veterans and related persons, and local residents, with a lease concluded after final selection. A 2008 practice direction treated public-area awards as administrative acts. A 2015 High Administrative Court decision treated such mayoral decisions as property management, and a 2019 Constitutional Court decision found no access-to-court violation. Administrative courts then declared related actions inadmissible between 2016 and 2020. In a 2020 decision, the Constitutional Court held that judicial protection had to be ensured for all individual acts of public authorities. From 2018 onwards, some administrative courts again treated grants of use of public areas as administrative acts and examined cases on the merits.
001-253222:
The applicants, Háttér Társaság and Amnesty International Hungary, are Hungarian organisations based in Budapest, represented by Mr Tordai. They complained of violations of their rights to freedom of expression and a fair trial arising from decisions of Hungary’s National Election Commission (“NEC”) fining them for campaigning for invalid ballots in a national referendum.

In July 2021 the Hungarian Government organised a referendum, stated to aim at protecting children’s best interests. It submitted five questions to the NEC. After legal challenges, the President of the Republic announced that the referendum would be held on 3 April 2022 with only the first four questions. The applicant organisations, together with twelve other civil-society organisations, campaigned encouraging voters to cast invalid ballots, arguing that the questions were misleading and promoted homophobic and transphobic policies. The referendum was held on 3 April 2022, the same day as a general election. About 1,700,000 voters cast invalid ballots, roughly 30% of ballots cast. The referendum results were invalid for all four questions because a majority of registered voters did not cast a valid vote.

Following a third-party complaint, the NEC found on 8 April 2022 (decision no. 324/2022) that the first applicant had infringed section 2(1)(e) of Act no. XXXVI of 2013 on Electoral Procedure (“EPA”), the principle of exercising rights in accordance with their purpose, by publishing Facebook posts calling for invalid ballots. The NEC fined it HUF 3,000,000 (about EUR 7,400). It reasoned that voters may cast invalid ballots, but a campaign encouraging this was incompatible with the referendum’s purpose and obstructed the people’s expression of will. On the same day, decision no. 328/2022 found that the applicant organisations operated the website ervenytelenul.hu, which called on voters to “Cast an invalid vote in response to an invalid question” and advised how to mark ballots invalid. The NEC found the same infringement but imposed no fine because the campaign period had ended.

The first applicant sought judicial review of the fine, arguing that referendum campaigns were a crucial forum for public affairs, that encouraging voters to cast a lawful invalid vote fell within highly protected expression, and that its conduct did not violate the purpose of referendum campaigning. In decision no. Kvk.IV.39.419/2022/4 of 13 April 2022, the Kúria rejected the claim without examining the merits, holding that the first applicant had failed to show specific grounds why the NEC’s interpretation was wrong or to identify the precise rights or values allegedly not balanced. Both applicants also challenged decision no. 328/2022, adding that restriction required a specific statutory basis and had to be necessary and proportionate, and that no provision prohibited encouraging invalid votes. In decision no. Kvk.IV.39.420/2022/4 of 13 April 2022, the Kúria dismissed the claim on the same grounds.

Each applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging infringement of freedom of expression under Article IX and fair trial under Article XXVIII of the Fundamental Law. They argued the Kúria failed to adjudicate the merits and ignored their arguments, and that the NEC’s restriction lacked legal basis and was disproportionate. On 22 April 2022, the Constitutional Court rejected the complaints (decisions nos. 3216/2022 and 3217/2022). It held that the fair-trial complaint raised no constitutional issue but challenged legality, and that the Kúria’s examination was a precondition for constitutional review of the expression issue.

The record also notes other NEC decisions of 8 April 2022: decision no. 325/2022 fined the second applicant HUF 3,000,000; decision no. 327/2022 fined the applicants and fourteen other organisations HUF 176,400 each; and decision no. 329/2022 found the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union had breached section 2(1)(e) but imposed no fine. On 15 April 2022, the Kúria overturned those decisions, holding that campaign activity formed part of protected expression, that no explicit statutory restriction existed, and that restrictions required constitutional and statutory grounds.
001-253224:
The applicant, Ersan Taş, is a Turkish national born in 1984 who lives in Istanbul. At the time of the events, he held a Twitter account named “@06melihchina,” followed by more than 55,000 users. The account was a parody account that portrayed jokes about İ.M.G., then mayor of Ankara.

On 24 September 2014, İ.M.G.’s official account on the same platform posted a photo and a mocking statement about K.K., then chairman of the main opposition party. On the same day, the applicant made a comment under that post. His comment included a derisive image pertaining to the President and İ.M.G., accompanied by the statement: “We continue to work and steal tirelessly with our President, God willing” (Cumhurbaşkanımızla birlikte hiç durmadan çalışmaya ve çalmaya devam ediyoruz Allah’ın izniyle).

On 17 December 2014, İ.M.G. filed a criminal complaint against the applicant concerning the content of his comment. On 26 September 2017, the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance sentenced the applicant to eleven months and twenty days’ imprisonment for insulting the President of the Republic and ten months’ imprisonment for insulting a public official on account of his functions. The Criminal Court suspended the pronouncement of the judgment under Article 231 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and imposed a five-year supervision period. On 9 November 2017, the Ankara Assize Court dismissed the applicant’s objection, finding that the decision had been made in accordance with procedural and substantial law.

On 20 December 2017, the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court. Relying on Article 10 of the Convention, he complained, among other things, about his conviction owing to the comment in question. On 29 March 2023, the Constitutional Court found a violation of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression in a judgment grouping similar applications, in accordance with its findings in the Atilla Yazar and Others judgment. To redress the violation, the Constitutional Court ordered a retrial and sent a copy of its judgment to the Criminal Court for the reopening of the criminal proceedings. It also ordered reimbursement of the court fees the applicant had paid before the Criminal Court, as well as his legal representation costs. However, it rejected his just satisfaction claims in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The decision was served on the applicant’s lawyer on 13 July 2023.

On 9 November 2023, the applicant introduced an application before the European Court. On the same day, he lodged a petition with the Criminal Court seeking a retrial to secure implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgment. On 12 December 2023, the Criminal Court rejected the applicant’s request in a final decision, stating that the Constitutional Court had not yet delivered its decision concerning the applicant’s individual application. On 15 November 2024, the Constitutional Court filed a petition with the Criminal Court requesting information on the retrial proceedings. On 21 November 2024, the Criminal Court informed the Constitutional Court that the retrial proceedings had not been commenced, without providing any reasons.

In his application to the Court, relying on Article 10 of the Convention, the applicant complained that his right to freedom of expression had been breached on account of his conviction and prison sentence, combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, owing to a comment he had posted on social media.
001-253230:
F.W., a Syrian national born in 1981 living in Madrid, has four children: A (girl, born 2010), B (boy, born 2011), C (boy, born 2016) and D (girl, born November 2018). A January 2019 certificate assessed F.W. as having 79% disability due to upper and lower limb limitations; other documents mentioned 86% or 88%. Child B has cerebral palsy, assessed at 76% in Türkiye in 2017 and 80% in Spain in 2023. In July 2017 F.W. and her family arrived in Spain from Türkiye under a resettlement programme, were granted subsidiary protection, and were housed in a refugee reception centre (CAR) in Madrid. On 27 July 2017 her then husband, I.A., slapped her in front of the children. He was convicted of domestic violence on 5 September 2017 and sentenced to nine months and one day; on 6 June 2018 the sentence was suspended with conditions, including no approach to or communication with F.W. The family left the CAR for Germany in September 2017, returned to Spain in April 2018, and stayed in a social emergency reception centre (SAMUR).

On 21 May 2018 SAMUR asked the Child Guardianship Authority to protect A, B and C, citing F.W.’s inability to carry out basic activities, her refusal of caregivers, A caring for her mother and B, I.A.’s expulsion from the centre, aggression, an accusation of sexual abuse of another resident, and inappropriate sexual behaviour towards A. On 22 May the DGFC began guardianship proceedings; on 24 May three decisions declared A, B and C in a situation of neglect and imposed provisional guardianship; on 25 May they were transferred to an initial protection centre; on 20 June weekend leave was refused; and on 4 July they moved to a child protection centre (CPC). D was born on 11 November 2018 and remained with F.W. under a protection file.

On 20 December 2018 F.W. sought revocation of the neglect decision and voluntary custody. She argued that her disability, lack of resources and status as a domestic-violence victim were not grounds for neglect, denied negligence, and requested more visits. Reports in 2019 noted a strong bond; Fundación Madrina considered she could care for the children with support. An October 2019 CAI report stated that the only elements preventing lifting the measure were her physical disability and high socio-economic vulnerability, and proposed a less restrictive measure. January 2020 DGFC reports proposed confirming guardianship. In February/March 2020 visits were suspended after alleged breach of the restraining order and unauthorised lessons. Application no. 23441/25 was lodged against Bulgaria with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 August 2025 by A.M., an Uzbek national born in 1981. He was represented by V. Petkov, a lawyer practising in Sofia. Bulgaria is the respondent State.

The applicant arrived in Bulgaria in August 2022 and applied for international protection in October 2022. The State Agency for Refugees (“SAR”) interviewed him and, under an accelerated procedure, rejected the application as manifestly unfounded. The Sofia City Administrative Court (“SCAC”) upheld that decision after he lodged a claim for judicial review.

In December 2022 the applicant lodged a subsequent application for international protection, enclosing an opinion by a psychologist he had consulted. The SAR rejected the application without an examination on the merits. The applicant sought judicial review, and the SCAC again upheld the SAR’s decision.

In April 2023 he lodged a second subsequent application for international protection. He enclosed a report by two forensic medical experts who had examined him and four documents he described as having been issued by the Uzbek authorities. The SAR rejected the application without examining it on the merits. The SCAC set that decision aside after the applicant lodged a judicial review claim. After interviewing the applicant, the SAR dismissed the application. The SCAC upheld that decision, and the Supreme Administrative Court (“SAC”) upheld the SCAC’s judgment on appeal.

In June 2025 the applicant lodged a third subsequent application for international protection. The SAR rejected it without considering it on the merits. The applicant sought judicial review of that decision but later withdrew his claim, and the SCAC discontinued the proceedings. He later stated that he wished to retract the withdrawal. The SCAC directed him to clarify whether that statement was intended as an appeal against the discontinuance. The applicant did not comply, and the discontinuance became final.

In February 2023, while the above applications were being processed, the migration authorities ordered the applicant’s return to Uzbekistan. He sought judicial review, but the SCAC upheld the order and the SAC upheld the SCAC’s judgment on appeal. He later sought to have the SAC proceedings reopened but abandoned that attempt.

In July 2025 the applicant was placed in immigration detention. Separately, after twice attempting to cross illegally into Romania in March and April 2025, he was sentenced in October 2025 to eighteen months’ imprisonment. He remained in prison serving that sentence until June 2026. He was then placed in immigration detention.

The applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that the Bulgarian authorities and courts had not properly assessed whether he would face a risk of ill-treatment if removed to Uzbekistan. He alleged that the risk was real and that, if he were removed, this would breach Article 3.
